$all = $errors->all();                 // Flat message list
$first = $errors->first();             // First message, or null
$email = $errors->first('email_address');
$messages = $errors->get('email_address'); // [] when absent
$hasError = $errors->has('email_address');
$map = $errors->toArray();
$json = json_encode($errors, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);

    Message precedence is concrete field.rule, declared wildcard pattern.rule, global rule, then the default English message. Attribute labels accept exact fields or the declared wildcard pattern. Supported placeholders are :attribute, :field, :rule, :min, :max, and :length. get()/first(field)/has() use exact concrete paths, not wildcard queries. The application translation service can supply these message and label maps; validator defaults remain in US English.

    Errors never automatically include submitted values. Messages are still plain, untrusted output: escape them in HTML, including application-provided labels. JSON serialization produces the field/message map (or {} when empty).

    Request, API, and exception integration

    PHP
    $data = $request->validate([
    'name' => 'required|string|max:100',
    'email' => 'required|email',
]);

    This validates the parsed body only, never query parameters or uploads implicitly. JSON capture now converts nested JSON objects to associative arrays for consistent dot-path validation. For query filters, explicitly build an array from $request->query().

    On failure, ValidationException exposes a ValidationErrors object as $exception->errors; it does not retain original input. API routes can call $request->validate() directly: existing API exception handling sends HTTP 422 using Osoni's established envelope, not a second response convention:

    JSON
    {
  "error": {
    "status": 422,
    "message": "Check your input.",
    "details": {
      "email": ["The email field must be a valid email value."]
    }
  }
}

    Api::validate($request, $rules, $messages, $attributes) uses the same engine but retains ApiValidationException for compatibility. Web application exception handling returns generic plain-text 422; form controllers can instead use fails()/errors()->toArray() or catch ValidationException to render field messages using their existing views. CSRF, authentication, rate limiting, and authorization remain separate.

    Imports, DTOs/models, and custom rules

    PHP
    $rows = \Osoni\FileReader::iterate($csvPath);
foreach ($rows as $row) {
    $data = Validator::make($row, [
        'email' => 'required|email',
        'age' => 'nullable|integer|min:18',
    ])->validate();
    // Apply business authorization and persistence explicitly.
}

    CSV values stay strings, so use integer/numeric when numeric bounds are intended. Blank CSV cells are empty strings, not null. JSON/YAML reader arrays work directly. XML's explicit node representation can be validated with matching paths or mapped to a simpler record first. Map DTO/model input explicitly to arrays; the validator never reflects into objects, invokes model hydration, or mass-assigns fields.

    Custom rules implement the small Osoni\RuleInterface:

    PHP
    final class VatNumberRule implements \Osoni\RuleInterface
{
    public function validate(string $field, mixed $value, array $data): bool
    {
        return is_string($value) && preg_match('/^NL[0-9]{9}B[0-9]{2}$/D', $value) === 1;
    }

    public function message(): string
    {
        return 'The :attribute value is not a valid VAT number.';
    }
}

$data = Validator::make($input, [
    'vat_number' => ['required', new VatNumberRule()],
])->validate();

    Explicitly require custom rule classes; there is no class discovery. Custom rules run for existing fields (including empty values), but skip allowed nullable nulls; use required for presence. They receive the concrete field, unchanged value, and original array. Business/database failures propagate rather than becoming successful defaults. A custom rule may accept an explicitly injected Database/repository for future unique/exists checks; the core never opens a connection. Enforce database uniqueness with database constraints as well, since validation alone cannot prevent races. No built-in database rule or SQL table name is inferred from untrusted input.

    Uploaded files

    When bootstrap has loaded the existing upload abstraction, explicitly pass the selected UploadedFile objects:

    PHP
    $data = Validator::make(['document' => $request->file('document')], [
    'document' => 'required|file|mimes:pdf|max_size:2097152',
])->validate();

    file, mimes, mimetypes, and max_size all reuse UploadedFile::validate(): actual HTTP-upload provenance, nonempty content, extension/MIME matching, supported image headers, and Office-package checks. mimes is an explicit comma-separated list from the existing supported extension allowlist. mimetypes accepts exact canonical detected MIME names, not wildcard patterns or the browser's claimed type. max_size is bytes. No file rule accepts a local path instead of an HTTP upload.

    File rules without a max_size impose no additional validator byte cap (PHP/web-server limits still apply). Supply a bound explicitly or use the existing Uploads service for configured environment limits. Unsupported upload formats remain unsupported. Content/type/size failures become field errors; server-side upload failures propagate normally. Validated output retains the same accepted object; storing/moving the file is a separate authorized operation.

    Boundaries

    Validation is not sanitization, output escaping, authorization, CSRF, or business correctness. Never interpolate validated values into SQL/shell code; retain parameter binding and context-appropriate escaping. Limits are 1000 field definitions, 32 path segments/512 bytes, and 100000 wildcard expansion steps. Bound incoming payloads/array sizes and trusted regex complexity at their own boundaries. Configuration errors and operational failures throw explicitly; they never become empty successful validation.

    Views and Validation

    Osoni Templates

    The native template engine supports layouts, sections, includes, components, slots, conditionals, and loops. No dependencies, eval(), or Composer: templates are compiled to PHP and executed with require.

    Terminal
    php osoni make:template messages.index
php osoni make:template layouts.blog
php osoni make:template components.panel

    messages.index refers to app/views/messages/index.osoni.php. Your controller continues to use the same API:

    PHP
    return new \Osoni\Response($this->app->views->render('messages.index', [
    'name' => 'My application',
    'title' => 'Messages',
    'items' => ['First message', 'Second message'],
    'session' => $this->app->session,
]));

    Data is available as ordinary PHP variables. Expressions use native PHP syntax, such as $title ?? 'Default title', strtoupper($name), or $item['title']. All {{ ... }} output is automatically HTML-escaped:

    HTML
    <h1>{{ $title }}</h1>
<input name="name" value="{{ $oldName ?? '' }}">
{{-- This comment does not appear in the HTML. --}}

    Use this for HTML text and quoted attributes. This does not replace URL validation, CSS escaping, or JavaScript encoding. Scalars, null, and Stringable are supported; arrays and other objects produce an error. Do not also use e() inside {{ }}, or you will double-escape.

    Unescaped HTML is explicit: {!! $html !!}. Use this only for trusted markup, such as an already rendered component slot, never for unsanitized user input or incoming email.

    Layouts and Sections

    A layout in app/views/layouts/blog.osoni.php:

    HTML
    <!doctype html>
<html lang="en-US">
<head><title>@yield('title', 'My blog')</title></head>
<body>
    @include('partials.header')
    <main>@yield('content')</main>
</body>
</html>

    And a page in app/views/messages/index.osoni.php:

    HTML
    @extends('layouts.blog')

@section('title')
{{ $title }}
@endsection

@section('content')
    <h1>{{ $title }}</h1>
    @if(empty($items))
        <p>There are no messages yet.</p>
    @else
        <ul>
        @foreach($items as $item)
            <li>{{ $item }}</li>
        @endforeach
        </ul>
    @endif
@endsection

    @section is always a block with @endsection; the inline form @section('title', 'Title') is not supported. @yield displays an already rendered section without additional escaping. The optional default value of @yield is escaped. A template with @extends may produce only whitespace outside sections. Layouts may themselves extend another layout; sections from the most specific page take precedence. A duplicate section in the same template is an error. Sections are never shared between requests or separate renders.

    Partials and Components

    An include inherits the variables in the current scope, including loop variables. Explicit data overrides inherited values only inside the include:

    HTML
    @include('partials.item', ['title' => $item])

    Includes have their own section context; define layout sections in the page itself, not in an include.

    Components receive only the explicit props and their rendered slots. For example, app/views/components/panel.osoni.php:

    HTML
    <section>
    <h2>{{ $title }}</h2>
    {!! $slot !!}
    @if(isset($footer))
        <footer>{!! $footer !!}</footer>
    @endif
</section>

    Usage:

    HTML
    @component('components.panel', ['title' => 'Latest messages'])
    <p>{{ $intro }}</p>
    @slot('footer')
        <a href="/berichten">All messages</a>
    @endslot
@endcomponent

    $slot contains the main content. Named slots such as $footer are made available separately and override any props with the same name. slot is reserved. Slot names are unique variable names without a leading underscore; an @slot must be directly inside a component. You can nest different components. Variables inside the invocation content come from the page, not from the component's props.

    Directives and Error Handling

    SyntaxUsage
    {{ $value }}HTML-escaped output
    {!! $html !!}Intentionally raw HTML
    {{-- ... --}}Template comment
    @extends('layouts.app')Extend a layout
    @section('name') ... @endsectionDefine a section
    @yield('name', 'default')Display a section, with optional default
    @include('partial', ['key' => $value])Partial with optional data
    @component('component', ['key' => $value]) ... @endcomponentComponent
    @slot('name') ... @endslotNamed component slot
    @if(...) ... @elseif(...) ... @else ... @endifConditionals
    @foreach($items as $item) ... @endforeachIterate over a collection
    @for($i = 0; $i < 3; $i++) ... @endforCounted loop
    @csrf($session)Secure hidden CSRF field

    Use @@ for a literal @, for example @@include. Separate directives without arguments from following letters with whitespace or HTML, for example @else <p>No results</p>. You can include regular email addresses as text; if an address happens to contain a directive name, write it as {{ 'name@if.example' }}. Do not use PHP tags, heredoc, or backtick expressions in Osoni templates; regular PHP views remain available for exceptions.

    Unknown directives, malformed expressions, and incorrectly nested blocks throw an exception with the template name. Missing views, cyclic layouts, recursive includes/components, and nesting beyond 32 views also produce an error. Output buffers are cleaned up after errors, without returning a partial page as a success. The existing application error handling displays a generic 500 in production and logs the error.

    Compilation and Cache

    The cache is in storage/views/ by default, outside public/. On Linux, the directory and new cache files get 0700 and 0600; on Windows, the folder's NTFS ACLs apply. Make sure the PHP service user can create and read this cache. Align ownership and permissions for the CLI and web server; never give uploaders write access to this directory.

    The cache name contains a hash of the template path, content, and compiler version. Changed templates are automatically recompiled, even when their modification time stays the same. Cache files contain only compiled code, not supplied view data or rendered pages. A lock and atomic publication protect concurrent compilations. Cached old content is not used if compilation fails. Old hashes remain until you clear the cache:

    Terminal
    php osoni view:clear

    This removes only compiled Osoni cache files, not your source templates or other files in storage/. Run this during deployment when workers/requests are inactive; do not delete code currently being loaded. For a custom View instance, you can pass the cache directory as the second constructor argument.

    The home page uses home.osoni.php, layouts.app, two partials, and components.feedback as a working example.

    Existing PHP Views

    php osoni make:view messages.index continues to generate a regular app/views/messages/index.php. When both formats exist, .osoni.php takes precedence; generators reject such naming conflicts. In regular PHP views, you still escape values yourself with e():

    PHP
    <h1><?= e($title) ?></h1>

    Security boundary: both template formats are trusted application code, not a sandbox for visitors. PHP expressions can execute PHP functions; never let visitors upload or modify templates or choose view paths. View data names beginning with __ are reserved for the engine.

    Validation in existing forms

    This section shows the backward-compatible static API used by existing forms. For expanded rules, nullable fields, nested arrays, filtered output, and custom rules, use the Validation Component.

    PHP
    $errors = \Osoni\Validator::errors($request->all(), [
    'name' => 'required|string|min:2|max:80',
    'email' => 'required|email',
    'age' => 'integer',
    'password' => 'required|string|min:12|confirmed',
]);

    errors() returns a list of English-language errors per field, or []. min and max check the number of Unicode characters in strings, not numeric values. Without required, fields may be missing or empty. confirmed compares against, for example, password_confirmation. Unknown or incorrectly configured rules throw an exception.

    Check $errors before saving your data. The example in HomeController returns status 422 for validation errors, displays errors by field, and preserves the input. For other forms, choose the same HTML approach yourself or a JSON response with status 422.

    Sessions and CSRF

    For browser routes, a session remembers data between visits, such as the logged-in user and form security tokens. By default, Osoni uses PHP's configured session handler, normally local files. The browser stores only a session-ID cookie, not the session's contents.

    Store sessions in the database

    Use this when multiple application servers need to share login sessions, or when you prefer database-managed storage. No extra PHP packages are needed; the driver uses the same database configured by DB_*.

    1. Keep SESSION_DRIVER=native while preparing the database.
    2. Run php osoni migrate to create the sessions table. For production, back up first and use the reviewed php osoni migrate --force command.
    3. Add these settings to your private .env, or edit their existing entries:
    Configuration
    SESSION_DRIVER=database
SESSION_LIFETIME=7200
SESSION_LOCK_TIMEOUT=10

    SESSION_LIFETIME is the idle timeout in seconds: 7200 is two hours. Each successful session save refreshes it, even if the data did not change. SESSION_LOCK_TIMEOUT is how many seconds a request waits for another request using the same session to finish (1 to 60; default 10). Native storage continues to use PHP's own expiry settings.

    Restart/reload your web service if its deployment requires configuration reloads. Sign in again and check that a row appears in sessions. Changing storage drivers does not transfer sessions; existing users must sign in again. To switch back, set SESSION_DRIVER=native. Do not roll back the sessions migration while the database driver is active.

    The table stores a SHA-256 hash of the session ID, a base64-encoded PHP session payload, and last_activity/expires_at Unix timestamps. Base64 is not encryption. Restrict database access and backups just as you would for login data. Do not print payloads in admin pages or logs. Session cookies remain HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and browser-session cookies; the idle timeout does not turn them into persistent "remember me" cookies. Keep SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true for production HTTPS.

    SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server are supported. Requests sharing a session are locked to avoid lost updates during simultaneous form or login requests. MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server use connection-scoped advisory locks on a dedicated connection; use direct or session-affine connections, not transaction-pooled PostgreSQL connections. SQL Server accounts need permission to use sp_getapplock/sp_releaseapplock. SQLite uses up to 256 private lock files in STORAGE_PATH/sessions; all processes using the same SQLite database must share that storage path. Use a server database for multi-node deployments, not SQLite on a network share. Do not delete lock files while requests are running.

    Expired sessions are rejected immediately on access. PHP's session.gc_probability / session.gc_divisor schedule removal of expired rows. If your PHP installation disables automatic cleanup, schedule a trusted CLI script that loads bootstrap.php, calls $app->session->start(), then session_gc(), and finally $app->session->close(). This removes expired rows only; it is not a command for logging everyone out.

    The framework saves sessions before sending responses, so a failed database write returns an error instead of appearing successful. Database outages and lock timeouts do not silently fall back to local files. Stateless API requests and health/readiness probes still do not start sessions; readiness checks the sessions table when database storage is selected.

    Protect browser forms with CSRF

    All browser-route POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests require a session token. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS carry no token, so the application never dispatches them to a route that only has handlers for methods which change data: such a request is refused with 405 and an Allow header. Do not modify data with GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS either; keep them on their own read routes.

    PHP
    <form action="/berichten" method="post">
    <?= csrf_field($session) ?>
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

    Pass $this->app->session to the view as session. A JSON client can send the same token as X-CSRF-Token, along with the session cookie. An incorrect or missing token returns 419. There are intentionally no default browser-route CSRF exceptions. Stateless API routes use bearer tokens rather than browser sessions or CSRF tokens. For a form with bot protection, also send the CAPTCHA fields and empty honeypot; a CSRF token alone is not sufficient.

    PHP
    $this->app->session->put('notice', 'Saved');
$notice = $this->app->session->get('notice');
$this->app->session->regenerate();

    Authentication automatically regenerates the session ID and CSRF token on login and logout, and Session::regenerate() rotates the token too. Existing session data is cleared at that time. A CSRF token does not replace access control; explicitly protect your routes.

    CAPTCHA and Honeypot

    The selected forms use both controls: registration, login, forgot password, verification-email resend, and the name form on the home page. Logout, confirming a verification link, and saving a new password remain protected by CSRF and their own guards/tokens and existing limits, without an additional CAPTCHA.

    The CAPTCHA is entirely native PHP: no external services, JavaScript, GD, fonts, Composer, or API key. GET /captcha/{id} returns a local SVG with six random characters, drawn as vector paths with light noise. The solution is not present as text or metadata in the HTML/SVG; the session stores its SHA-256 hash, along with the SVG, form name, and expiration time. Ambiguous characters 0, 1, I, and O are not used.

    User Experience

    • Enter the six characters; capitalization does not matter. Leading and trailing spaces are ignored.
    • A code is valid for five minutes and works only in the same session and for the same form purpose.
    • Each submission attempt consumes the supplied code, even with an incorrect answer, a filled honeypot, or another validation error. The form then displays a new code; password fields remain empty.
    • Show another code refreshes through a CSRF-protected POST without performing the form action, logging in, or sending email. The browser does not need to validate other fields first. Name/email values are preserved; passwords are not. The form's old code is revoked.
    • Fetching images or making HEAD requests does not consume a code. Images are session-bound and are not cached.
    • Up to twelve unexpired codes per session support multiple tabs. If there are more, the oldest code expires. Up to sixty new codes per session per minute; after that, 429 with Retry-After is returned.
    • The website honeypot must be present as an empty string. The field is visually hidden, removed from the tab order, and hidden from screen readers; autocomplete is disabled. Filled, missing, or incorrectly typed values are rejected.

    Bot-check errors return 422 with a generic message and a new form. Missing/incorrect CSRF remains 419 and is checked earlier. No success message is displayed for a blocked action. The existing database-backed authentication limits remain active when the bot check passes.

    Limitations: a simple SVG CAPTCHA can be solved by OCR, pattern recognition, or human-solving services. The honeypot is an additional hurdle, not proof that a visitor is human. The creation limit is session-bound; new cookies bypass that limit. Also use request limits per IP and abuse detection on your trusted web server/proxy. A visual CAPTCHA is not independently usable by blind users: there is no audio or equivalent accessible verification route yet. Provide one before offering these forms to an audience for whom visual verification is inaccessible; do not add an unprotected bypass.

    Custom Forms

    The existing Application exposes $app->botProtection:

    PHP
    // When displaying the form, after any session/auth checks:
$captcha = $app->botProtection->challenge('contact');

// Pass captcha and errors to a Osoni view, plus session for @csrf.
// In the form:
// @csrf($session)
// @include('partials.bot-protection')

// In a POST handler, after the global CSRF check:
$errors = $app->botProtection->errors($request, 'contact');
if ($errors !== []) {
    // Render status 422, with errors and a new challenge('contact').
    // Do not perform the actual form action here.
}

    Choose a fixed server-side form name yourself, not a purpose from request input. Reuse that exact name for issuing and checking. The partial contains _captcha_id, _captcha_answer, and website. As in the existing views, place the refresh button _captcha_refresh=1 with formnovalidate after your normal submit button, so Enter submits the form by default instead of only refreshing the code. Handle refresh separately before the actual action: $app->botProtection->forget($request, 'contact'), create a new challenge, and render the form again. Your own handlers do not get bot protection automatically.

    The existing session storage must be server-side and private. Login/logout clears all session data, including any open CAPTCHAs. A JSON client uses the same field names, same cookies, and existing CSRF header; there is intentionally no test mode or API exception that skips CAPTCHA. Tests create a known solution only in their isolated, local session fixture; this does not change production code.

    Authentication

    Run php osoni migrate to create users, auth_tokens, auth_limits, auth_mfa, and auth_mfa_recovery (plus the other framework tables). Also set the public origin in your existing .env:

    DOTENV
    APP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000

    In production, this might be https://app.example.com: HTTPS is required, with no path, username, query, or fragment. HTTP is allowed only locally on localhost. Links are built only from this configuration, never from incoming Host or proxy headers. If you use a different local port, update APP_URL.

    Pages and Flow

    RoutePurpose
    GET/POST /registerCreate an account and queue a verification email
    GET/POST /loginSign in with an email address and password
    GET/POST /login/mfaComplete a pending MFA login with an authenticator or recovery code
    POST /logoutClear the session, regenerate ID and CSRF
    GET/POST /forgot-passwordRequest a reset link
    GET/POST /reset-passwordChoose a new password with a token
    GET/POST /verify-emailVerify an email address and establish the owner's password with a token
    GET /email/verifyVerification notice for signed-in users
    POST /email/verification-notificationRequest a new verification email
    GET /accountExample page requiring login and email verification
    GET /account/mfaSet up or manage optional per-user MFA
    POST /account/mfa/setupConfirm the current password and start authenticator enrollment
    POST /account/mfa/confirmConfirm enrollment and display recovery codes once
    POST /account/mfa/disableDisable MFA with the current password and an unused second-factor code
    GET/POST /account/mfa/recovery-codesConfirm both factors, replace recovery codes, and display the new codes once

    Saving application data at registration: In your registration controller, validate any additional fields before calling register() so field errors are handled the same way for new and existing email addresses. Pass the validated fields to an optional callback and use the provided Database instance to write to a table created by your application's migrations:

    PHP
    $app->auth->register(
    $request->all(),
    $request->clientIp(),
    static function (int $userId, \Osoni\Database $db) use ($validatedProfile): void {
        $db->insert('user_profiles', ['user_id' => $userId] + $validatedProfile, null);
    },
);

    The callback runs only for a new user, after verification mail is queued and before the transaction commits. If it throws, the exception propagates and the account, verification token, queued email, and callback writes roll back. Callbacks must not start nested transactions, commit or roll back themselves, or perform external side effects such as sending mail or making HTTP requests. Two-argument calls still work, and the controller should return the same generic success message for new and existing email addresses.

    After registration, sign in; unverified accounts are sent to the verification page. Open the verification link and choose and confirm the password to use from then on. The POST confirmation replaces the registration password, increments the account's session version, and revokes existing authentication and API tokens. All earlier login sessions become invalid, and the requester is signed out. This prevents someone who registered your email with their own password from retaining access after you verify ownership. Sign in again with your chosen password; verification does not sign you in automatically.

    A mail scanner opening the link with GET or HEAD does not consume it. Missing or invalid passwords do not consume a valid link. Invalid/expired tokens return 400, validation errors 422, too many attempts 429, and missing/incorrect CSRF 419.

    Verification API upgrade: custom callers must now pass password and password confirmation as the third argument:

    PHP
    $app->auth->verifyEmail($request->input('token'), $request->clientIp(), $request->all());

    Token-only calls intentionally fail. Update custom verification forms and controllers together; existing unexpired links can still be used with the updated form. Already-verified accounts are not automatically remediated: if pre-registration abuse may have occurred, investigate affected accounts, revoke their sessions/tokens, and have their email owners establish new passwords through a trusted recovery process.

    Passwords require at least 12 characters and no more than 72 bytes (the native bcrypt limit), plus a matching confirmation. They are not repopulated in forms, emailed, or stored other than using password_hash()/bcrypt, cost 12. Login uses password_verify() and rehashing when needed. Email addresses are ASCII and are trimmed and lowercased; name and other fields are not automatically copied to database fields.

    Optional Authenticator MFA

    The included account pages support time-based one-time passwords (TOTP), compatible with authenticator apps that support SHA-1, six digits, and a 30-second period. Existing accounts keep password-only login until their verified owner enables MFA.

    Enrollment and Emergency Enforcement Policy

    Both settings default to true, preserving existing behavior. Bootstrap reads them through config/auth.php:

    Configuration
    AUTH_MFA_ENROLLMENT_ENABLED=true
AUTH_MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=true
    • Enrollment: setting AUTH_MFA_ENROLLMENT_ENABLED=false rejects both starting and confirming new setup with 403, including setup started before the change. It does not erase enrollment, secrets, or recovery codes. Enrolled users are still challenged when enforcement is enabled and can manage, regenerate recovery codes, or disable MFA with the usual password and second-factor checks. Account pages explain the unavailable state rather than offering new setup; enrolled users retain their management and recovery-code replacement links.
    • Emergency enforcement: setting AUTH_MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=false bypasses the local MFA challenge for every new password or OIDC login. Correct password/provider authentication, rate limits, email-verification guards, and session-version checks still apply. Encrypted secrets, accepted authenticator counters, and recovery-code hashes remain intact. Management actions still require the current password and an unused second factor. Enrollment remains independently controlled.

    Disabling enforcement weakens every enrolled account's login protection. Use it only as a controlled, temporary emergency measure, not normal recovery for one user. Restrict access during the incident and restore true promptly. An attacker who can authenticate with the remaining first factor can obtain a full browser session while enforcement is off.

    Policy changes do not revoke existing authenticated sessions or API tokens, increment session versions, or retroactively challenge logged-in users. Sessions created during a bypass remain authorized after enforcement is restored until normal expiry or explicit revocation. Use a reviewed administrative session-version revocation procedure where required. Existing pending login challenges are not promoted to full sessions when enforcement is disabled: complete the challenge normally, or start a fresh password/OIDC login under the new policy. Existing pending enrollment cannot be confirmed while enrollment is disabled.

    After every policy change, restart all application processes on every instance, including persistent PHP/web processes and CLI workers. Do not mix processes running different policies. Settings are loaded when each Application/Auth instance is constructed, not refreshed on each method call. Restarting alone does not revoke sessions. Invalid or empty environment values abort bootstrap instead of silently bypassing MFA; use true or false (case-insensitive).

    Applications constructing Application directly can supply actual PHP booleans in $config['auth']['mfa_enrollment_enabled'] and $config['auth']['mfa_enforcement_enabled']; omitted keys default to true. Strings, integers, arrays, and explicit null values are rejected. Direct Auth construction has optional trailing mfaEnrollmentEnabled and mfaEnforcementEnabled boolean parameters, both defaulting to true. Use the configured $app->auth for every authentication entry point.

    Enabling MFA

    1. Apply pending migrations with php osoni migrate. On an existing deployment, back up the database and follow the normal production migration procedure.
    2. Ensure a valid APP_KEY is configured. For a new installation only, run php osoni key:generate and copy its printed assignment into your private .env. Never replace an existing key to enable MFA. Back up the key; losing it prevents decrypting enrolled authenticator secrets.
    3. Log in, open My account, and choose Set up multi-factor authentication. Enter your current password, then scan the QR code with your authenticator app or manually add the displayed Base32 key. The QR code is generated locally, never sent to a QR service or embedded in a public image URL. On the same device, the authenticator link can open a compatible app.
    4. Enter a code from the app within ten minutes to enable MFA. Save the ten recovery codes shown on the confirmation page. They are displayed only once, and each code can replace an authenticator code once.

    The QR code contains the same secret as the manual setup key. Do not share either one, upload a screenshot to another service, or include it in support requests. You do not need a QR-code package, browser script, image extension, CDN, or separate QR endpoint. Keep the white border around the code intact when customizing its appearance.

    Enabling, disabling, or regenerating MFA recovery codes rotates the current session/CSRF token and invalidates other sessions and existing API tokens through the account's session version. The current browser stays logged in. Enabling MFA consumes the enrollment code, so wait for the next app code before using it again.

    Signing In and Using Recovery Codes

    1. Submit your email address and password on /login as usual.
    2. On Verify your login, enter the current six-digit authenticator code, including any leading zero. If your authenticator is unavailable, enter one unused recovery code in the same Authenticator or recovery code field. Copy the full 20-character lowercase hexadecimal recovery code exactly, without spaces.
    3. Select Verify and log in. A successful challenge opens your account. Mark a recovery code as used after it succeeds; it cannot be used again.

    Using a recovery code does not disable MFA or replace your authenticator. Recovery codes cannot confirm the initial enrollment, which requires an app-generated six-digit code.

    With enforcement enabled, password or OIDC login for an enrolled account creates only a pending challenge, not an authenticated user. Complete /login/mfa within five minutes; protected routes remain inaccessible until then. Successful completion clears pending state and rotates the session and CSRF token again. Canceling the challenge clears the pending login. There are no trusted-device or remember-MFA cookies.

    Disabling MFA or Replacing an Authenticator

    1. While fully logged in with a verified email address, open My account and select Manage multi-factor authentication.
    2. Enter your current password and an unused authenticator or recovery code, then select Disable multi-factor authentication.
    3. To replace an authenticator, select Set up multi-factor authentication and enroll again. Add the new QR code or key to your app and save the new recovery codes.

    Disabling deletes the old enrollment and its remaining recovery codes. The old authenticator entry no longer works after re-enrollment; remove it from your app once the replacement is confirmed. New enrollment must be allowed by policy before you can enroll the replacement.

    Regenerating Recovery Codes

    On My account, choose Manage multi-factor authentication, then Regenerate recovery codes without disabling MFA. Review the warning, enter your current password and an unused authenticator or recovery code, and choose Replace my recovery codes. Save the ten new codes immediately: the old codes stop working, but your authenticator stays unchanged. Canceling returns to settings without changing anything.

    The form at GET /account/mfa/recovery-codes never generates or displays saved codes. Only its CSRF-protected POST can replace them. The success response shows the new codes once, uses no-store/no-referrer, and never stores plaintext codes in session/flash data. The rotated CSRF token rejects resubmission of the original form. Revisiting the form does not retrieve the codes.

    Custom application handlers can use the same service API:

    PHP
    $recoveryCodes = $app->auth->regenerateMfaRecoveryCodes(
    $request->input('password'),
    $request->input('code'),
    $request->clientIp(),
);

    Call this service API only from an explicitly registered, verified-owner, CSRF-protected POST handler using $app->auth->protect(...), as the built-in account route does. Prompt for the current password and a current authenticator code or an unused recovery code; a pending login, guest, unverified user, or unenrolled account cannot regenerate codes. OIDC-only users must establish a local password through the existing trusted password-reset flow before password-confirmed management.

    On success, the method returns ten new random 20-character lowercase hexadecimal codes. Render them once for the current user, with Cache-Control: no-store and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, and require the user to save them securely. Never log, email, put them in a URL, or retain plaintext codes in session/flash storage. The database stores only SHA-256 hashes. The plaintext list cannot be retrieved again; a page refresh must not trigger another regeneration.

    The supplied second factor is consumed, all old recovery codes become invalid, and only the new hashes are inserted, in one transaction. Any failure rolls back the consumed code/authenticator counter, recovery hashes, and session version. The authenticator secret stays unchanged; accepted TOTP counters cannot be replayed. Password confirmation shares the existing password limits, and second-factor attempts share the login/enrollment/disable limits, even across sessions. Invalid factors and failures do not reset rate-limit counters.

    Successful regeneration increments the session version, invalidates other sessions, pending challenges/setup, and existing API tokens, and rotates the current session/CSRF token while keeping its owner logged in. Neither policy switch bypasses management factor checks. If delivery of the success page fails after commit, the old codes are already invalid: authenticate with the still-enrolled authenticator and regenerate again as needed.

    Security and Recovery Limits

    Authenticator verification allows one adjacent 30-second step in either direction for clock drift. Keep the server and device clocks synchronized. Accepted counters cannot be reused, including across browsers; accepting a future counter also blocks earlier ones. Secrets (including pending setup) use authenticated encryption bound to the user ID. Only SHA-256 hashes of the 80-bit random recovery codes are stored. Protect setup keys, recovery codes, session storage, the database, and backups; never log them.

    Password reset does not remove MFA and invalidates pending login/setup state through the session version. If both the authenticator and all recovery codes are lost, there is no self-service bypass. An administrator must use a separately designed, trusted identity-recovery procedure; no unauthenticated MFA-reset endpoint is included. Stateless API bearer authentication remains separate: newly issued tokens do not prompt for TOTP, so keep token issuance restricted to trusted administrators or fully authenticated, authorized application flows.

    Custom Login and Enrollment Pages

    For custom browser controllers, retain CSRF protection and the same session:

    In your existing login POST handler, after the CAPTCHA check:

    PHP
    $app->auth->login($request->all(), $request->clientIp());
return \Osoni\Response::redirect(
    $app->auth->mfaPending() ? '/login/mfa' : '/account'
);

    In a separate CSRF-protected second-step POST handler:

    PHP
    $app->auth->completeMfaLogin(['code' => $request->input('code')], $request->clientIp());
return \Osoni\Response::redirect('/account');

    login() still returns void: custom callers must not assume a successful password check means the user is authenticated. Use mfaPending() to choose the challenge and user()/protect() to authorize access.

    For a custom enrollment page, call beginMfaSetup() only in an authenticated, email-verified, CSRF-protected POST handler after the owner submits their current password. Generate its QR markup with \Osoni\QrCode::svg($setup['uri']) and pass that string to your view as qrSvg, alongside the setup data. Bootstrap already loads QrCode; it is a static utility, not an $app->qr service.

    In your custom .osoni.php enrollment template, render only the SVG returned by this utility as trusted markup:

    HTML
    <div class="mfa-qr">{!! $qrSvg !!}</div>
<p>Manual setup key: <code>{{ $setup['secret'] }}</code></p>

    Keep the response private with Cache-Control: no-store and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, retain the manual key and confirmation form, and call confirmMfaSetup() in a separate protected POST. Creating or scanning a QR code alone does not enable MFA.

    QrCode::svg() also accepts other printable ASCII payloads of 1-2953 bytes. It returns an inline black-on-white SVG using QR Model 2, byte mode, error correction level L, automatic version/mask selection, and a four-module white border. Empty, oversized, control-character, or non-ASCII input throws InvalidArgumentException. Percent-encoded authenticator URIs fit this input format; arbitrary Unicode text must not be passed directly. The utility does not authorize requests or protect where callers save the SVG.

    Sending Email

    Authentication emails always go through the existing database queue, even if MAIL_LOG=false. Configure MAIL_FROM and SMTP as described below, and run this regularly through cron or Windows Task Scheduler:

    Terminal
    php osoni mail:work 50

    Successful submission means the email is queued, not that it has been delivered. Without working SMTP configuration/worker, the user receives no email. No external email is sent during installation or tests. New accounts and their verification email are stored together: if queuing fails, registration is rolled back. Database and configuration errors are logged as server errors, not displayed as successful submissions.

    Tokens contain 32 cryptographically random bytes and are stored only as SHA-256 hashes in auth_tokens. Verification tokens are valid for 24 hours, reset tokens for 30 minutes, measured from the request. They are single-use; a new request replaces the previous link for the same purpose. The worker must therefore run promptly. Reset invalidates all existing login sessions for the account and signs out the requester. Reset does not automatically verify the email address.

    Warning: the sendable email in emails necessarily contains the full link. Protect the database, backups, and CLI access as secrets. Delete old emails according to your retention policy and configure web server/proxy logs not to retain token-bearing query strings. Authentication pages use no-store and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. Disable debug in production.

    Branded Authentication Emails

    By default, reset and verification emails keep the built-in plain-text subject and body. To customize them without editing framework code, register an application-owned composer in config/auth.php. Bootstrap loads this configuration for both browser requests and CLI commands before constructing $app->auth; no controller or mail-worker changes are needed.

    Create app/mail/auth-email.php (create the app/mail directory first):

    PHP
    <?php
declare(strict_types=1);

return static function (string $purpose, string $actionUrl, int $validForSeconds): array {
    $brand = 'Example Company';
    $action = match ($purpose) {
        'reset' => 'Reset your password',
        'verify' => 'Verify your email address',
        default => throw new InvalidArgumentException('Unsupported authentication email purpose.'),
    };
    $validity = match ($validForSeconds) {
        1800 => '30 minutes',
        86400 => '24 hours',
        default => "$validForSeconds seconds",
    };
    $escape = static fn (string $value): string =>
        htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, 'UTF-8');
    $notice = "This link is valid for $validity and can only be used once. "
        . 'If you did not request this, ignore this email.';

    return [
        'subject' => "$brand: $action",
        'text' => "$brand\n\n$action\n\n$actionUrl\n\n$notice",
        'html' => '<!doctype html><html lang="en-US"><body>'
            . '<h1>' . $escape($brand) . '</h1>'
            . '<p><a href="' . $escape($actionUrl) . '">' . $escape($action) . '</a></p>'
            . '<p>' . $escape($notice) . '</p></body></html>',
    ];
};

    In config/auth.php, keep the policy parsing and validation, and replace only the final return statement with:

    PHP
    return [
    'email_composer' => require dirname(__DIR__) . '/app/mail/auth-email.php',
] + $policy;

    The callable receives purpose **reset or verify**, the complete action URL derived from trusted APP_URL (not request headers), and validity in seconds: 1800 for reset, 86400 for verification. It runs for registration, verification resend, and password recovery only when an email is actually needed. Duplicate registration and unknown recovery addresses retain their generic responses and do not invoke it.

    Return exactly three string fields: subject, text, and html. Osoni validates them using the existing mail rules, including UTF-8, size limits, and subject header-injection rejection. Returning both bodies produces multipart/alternative on delivery; html => '' keeps a custom message plain-text only. Set email_composer back to null to restore the built-in messages. Applications constructing Application themselves can supply the same callable as $config['auth']['email_composer'].

    The composer owns HTML escaping: Osoni does not sanitize or autoescape the returned markup. Escape all dynamic HTML text and attribute values, including the URL, as shown above. Keep the plain-text body and subject as plain strings, not HTML-escaped strings. Preserve the supplied action URL and describe its actual validity and one-time use; do not reconstruct it from user-controlled hosts or add external tracking resources.

    Composition and mail validation happen inside the existing token-and-queue transaction. Exceptions and malformed results propagate as server errors, not successful submissions or a fallback email. They roll back the new token and queued mail, restore any replaced token, and also roll back a new registration. Rate-limit counters remain in force. Do not start/commit transactions or perform external side effects in the composer; keep it limited to rendering trusted local templates/strings. Never log its arguments, returned bodies, or token-bearing URLs, including in custom exception messages. The configured sender and actual recipient remain under Osoni's control. The worker sends the already composed content; token generation, expiry, consumption, and delivery policy are unchanged.

    Protecting Custom Routes

    PHP
    $router->get('/dashboard', $app->auth->protect([$controller, 'dashboard']));

// Exception: require login only, for example, on the verification page.
$router->get('/onboarding', $app->auth->protect([$controller, 'onboarding'], false));

$user = $app->auth->user();
// null or: id, name, email, email_verified_at; never a password hash.

    The guard redirects guests to /login and unverified accounts to /email/verify. There is no automatic redirect back to a supplied URL. Also protect your POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE routes with the guard. Existing example routes remain public and work without auth tables as long as there is no signed-in session. Per-object permissions and remember-me are not included; add authorization before exposing user data. Optional external login is described in the Single Sign-On chapter below.

    Role-Based Authorization

    Run php osoni migrate before using roles. Applications define their own role names and assign them only through trusted server-side code; registration and SSO do not grant any roles automatically. Do not accept a role assignment from an untrusted request or expose an assignment endpoint without its own authorization. A user may have multiple roles.

    PHP
    // Trusted administration or a seeder, after identifying an existing user.
$app->roles->assign($userId, 'admin');
$app->roles->has($userId, 'admin'); // true
$app->roles->revoke($userId, 'admin');

// In routes/web.php; requires a verified session and the admin role.
$router->get('/admin', $app->auth->protect([$controller, 'index'], role: 'admin'));

// In an API route module; requires a bearer token and the admin role.
$api->add('GET', '/api/admin', $handler, [
    'summary' => 'Admin report',
    'operationId' => 'adminReport',
    'responses' => ['200' => ['description' => 'Report']],
], role: 'admin');

    Role names are 1–64 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, starting with a letter. Duplicate assignments and missing users fail; revoking an absent assignment throws RecordNotFoundException. Role checks read the database on every guarded request, so changes affect existing sessions and tokens on the next check. Deleting a user deletes their role assignments. Guests and unverified users retain the normal web redirects; an authenticated user without the required role receives 403. The API returns 401 for a missing or invalid token and 403 for a valid user without the role. Role-protected operations document 403 and x-required-role in OpenAPI. Roles do not grant record ownership, protect existing routes automatically, or replace CSRF and per-record authorization.

    Sessions expire after 30 minutes of inactivity or a maximum of 12 hours from login. Each check reads the current user and session version from the database. Deleted users and sessions with an outdated version lose access.

    Fixed, database-backed time windows limit attempts, including across sessions:

    ActionLimit
    Registration5 per IP per hour
    Login10 per email address and 40 per IP per 15 minutes
    SSO callback40 per IP per 15 minutes
    Reset link5 per email address and 20 per IP per hour
    Submit reset20 per IP per hour
    Resend verification email5 per user and 20 per IP per hour
    Submit verification token30 per IP per 15 minutes
    MFA code (login, enrollment, disabling, or recovery-code regeneration)5 per user and 30 per IP per 5 minutes, shared across those actions
    MFA password confirmation (setup, disabling, or recovery-code regeneration)10 per user and 30 per IP per 15 minutes

    Requests that are invalid in content also count toward the IP limit once the CAPTCHA and honeypot have passed. Expired limit records are cleaned up on the next attempt. Only SHA-256 buckets are retained; raw IP addresses are not stored in auth_limits. The source is exclusively REMOTE_ADDR; forwarded headers are not trusted. Users behind a reverse proxy may share one limit: configure the real client IP only on a trusted web server/proxy, and also apply rate limiting at the edge. Registration and reset return the same message for existing and nonexistent accounts; these messages do not prevent analysis of timing or email delivery.

    Single Sign-On (SSO) (optional)

    Osoni supports optional OpenID Connect (OIDC) login alongside local accounts, using one configured provider per installation. Keycloak, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, Authentik, and other providers can be configured when they meet the protocol requirements below. Provider-specific live certification is not implied.

    Configure a provider

    1. Run php osoni migrate against your reviewed application database to add auth_identities. Back up production data and follow the normal migration deployment procedure.
    2. Register a web application at your identity provider. Enable authorization code flow, PKCE with S256, RS256 ID-token signing, and the scopes openid email profile. Register the exact redirect URI https://app.example.com/sso/callback; replace the origin with your own trusted HTTPS origin. Wildcards are not needed.
    3. Edit your private .env, or set process environment variables:
    DOTENV
    APP_URL=https://app.example.com
SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true
SSO_ENABLED=true
SSO_NAME="Company login"
SSO_ISSUER=https://identity.example.com/realms/company
SSO_CLIENT_ID=osoni
SSO_CLIENT_SECRET=replace-with-your-private-client-secret
SSO_TIMEOUT=10
SSO_CA_FILE=

    Keep the real client secret out of source control. Native cURL, OpenSSL, and the normal framework extensions are required; no Composer package is used. The issuer must exactly match discovery and ID-token iss, including any trailing slash. Osoni discovers endpoints from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration. All endpoints and APP_URL must use HTTPS, even for local SSO testing. Trust only administrator-controlled issuers and their discovery endpoints; they determine outbound destinations. SSO_CA_FILE optionally selects a readable local CA bundle without disabling certificate or hostname verification. Construction does not contact the provider.

    ProviderIssuer and setup notes
    KeycloakUse the realm issuer, normally https://host/realms/realm. Enable the client authentication mode matching your secret and S256 PKCE.
    Microsoft Entra IDUse a tenant-specific v2.0 issuer, normally https://login.microsoftonline.com/TENANT-ID/v2.0, not common or organizations. Register a Web redirect URI. Standard Entra tokens generally do not supply email_verified=true; pre-link accounts as described below rather than treating email or preferred_username as verified.
    OktaUse the exact authorization-server issuer from its discovery document; an organization issuer and /oauth2/default are different. Enable the requested scopes and email claims.
    Google WorkspaceUse https://accounts.google.com and a Web application client. Limit access to the intended organization in provider policy; an email domain or login-screen hint alone is not authorization.
    AuthentikUse the exact issuer advertised by the application's OpenID configuration. Configure signing keys, S256 PKCE, and email/profile scope mappings.

    Client authentication uses client_secret_basic when advertised (or when the discovery list is absent), otherwise client_secret_post. A client without a secret is accepted only when discovery explicitly advertises none. Private-key JWT, encrypted ID tokens, algorithms other than RS256, SAML, implicit flow, and form_post callbacks are not implemented.

    Browser flow and account policy

    With SSO enabled, /login displays Continue with Company login above the unchanged local login form. The button submits a CSRF-protected POST /sso/login. The provider returns a query-mode GET /sso/callback. This callback is the protocol-specific exception to mutation-free GETs: a session-bound, single-use state, nonce, and PKCE verifier protect it. HEAD is rejected without consuming the pending login. Starting a new SSO attempt replaces the previous one in that browser session; attempts expire after ten minutes.

    Osoni validates the RSA signature against newly fetched provider JWKS, exact issuer, audience/authorized party, expiry, issue time, optional not-before, nonce, and optional access-token/code hash claims. A failure consumes the pending attempt; restart from /login. Provider error descriptions, codes, and tokens are not echoed. Responses are capped at 1 MiB and each HTTPS request has the configured 1..60-second deadline; redirects are not followed.

    • Identities are keyed by the exact issuer + subject, not email. Existing mappings continue to select the same account even if provider profile/email claims change. Local profile data is not silently overwritten.
    • A new identity creates an account only with a valid ID-token email and the boolean claim email_verified=true. It receives a random, unknown password hash and a verified local email; no verification email is sent.
    • An email matching an existing local account is never automatically linked, even when the provider marks the email verified. Use local login and contact an administrator for deliberate linking.
    • Enrolled local MFA requires its usual authenticator or recovery code after provider login when AUTH_MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=true (the default). The emergency enforcement bypass applies equally to OIDC and password login. SSO does not issue API bearer tokens or bypass account session-version checks. Resetting a local password does not delete the mapping or enrolled MFA.
    • A provisioned user can use the existing password-reset email flow to establish a local password, including for password-confirmed MFA setup. Mail must be configured and processed. Keep local recovery access protected.
    • Logging out ends the Osoni browser session only. Provider logout, global logout, directory synchronization, and automatic revocation of existing Osoni sessions after provider disablement are not implemented. Revoke local sessions through the account's session version when required.

    Deliberately link an existing account

    There is no public linking/unlinking endpoint. A trusted administrator must independently verify ownership of both identities and obtain the exact stable OIDC sub for this client from the provider, not an email address or display name. In reviewed, private administrative PHP code after loading bootstrap:

    PHP
    // Trusted, independently verified administrative inputs, never request fields.
$issuer = 'https://identity.example.com/realms/company';
$subject = 'exact-provider-subject';
$userId = 42;
$app->db->insert('auth_identities', [
    'identity_hash' => hash('sha256', json_encode([$issuer, $subject], JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR)),
    'issuer' => $issuer,
    'subject' => $subject,
    'user_id' => $userId,
], null);

    Run this only after checking the target user and provider ownership. Existing unverified local accounts remain unverified and still require the local verification flow. A unique identity cannot be linked to two users; foreign keys remove mappings when their user is deleted. Remove a mapping by its exact identity hash through reviewed administrative code; do not rewrite applied migrations. SSO does not grant application roles or record ownership.

    Keep callback query strings out of proxy/server/access logs and protect session storage, identity tables, client secrets, and backups. SSO pages/redirects use no-store and no-referrer. Use provider-side access policies and edge rate limits. Disable the feature with SSO_ENABLED=false to hide the button and reject new SSO attempts; this does not remove accounts, mappings, or existing local sessions. The native suite uses isolated signed-token fixtures, not real provider calls. Validate your provider, claims, TLS, tenant restrictions, and deployment end to end before production.

    Database and Models

    DOTENV
    DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_DATABASE=osoni
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=osoni
DB_PASSWORD="your own password"

    Create the MySQL database and a separate user yourself. MySQL uses utf8mb4 and real prepared statements; use InnoDB for transactions. SQLite has foreign keys and a busy timeout enabled.

    PHP
    $rows = $app->db->execute(
    'SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE title = ?',
    [$title],
)->fetchAll();

$app->db->transaction(static function (\PDO $pdo): void {
    // Database work only; an exception causes a rollback.
});

    Always bind values; never concatenate user input into SQL. Table names, column names, and sort directions cannot be bound: use a fixed whitelist for those. Avoid nested transactions and DDL in Database::transaction().

    app/models/Note.php preserves the existing small repository API and uses the query builder internally:

    PHP
    require_once $app->root . '/app/models/Note.php';
$notes = new \App\Models\Note($app->db);
$id = $notes->create('My first note');
$recent = $notes->latest(20);

    Direct PDO remains available alongside the optional ORM.

    PostgreSQL

    PostgreSQL is supported through the native pdo_pgsql PHP extension and libpq on Windows and Linux, without Composer. Enable the extension in both CLI and web PHP. The shipped PostgreSQL schema uses identity columns; use a maintained PostgreSQL release. CI is configured to exercise PostgreSQL 16.

    Create a UTF-8 database and a dedicated login yourself. Use a least-privilege application role; migrations also need schema creation/drop permissions. Keep the same trusted search_path for CLI and web connections, normally public. Do not allow untrusted users to create objects in that schema. Update the existing .env entries rather than adding duplicate keys:

    DOTENV
    DB_CONNECTION=pgsql
DB_HOST=postgres.example.test
DB_PORT=5432
DB_DATABASE=osoni
DB_USERNAME=osoni
DB_PASSWORD="your own password"
DB_SSLMODE=verify-full
DB_SSLROOTCERT=/path/to/trusted-root.crt

    DB_SSLROOTCERT is optional: empty uses libpq's default root-certificate lookup. On Windows, use forward-slash paths such as C:/certificates/root.crt. The default verify-full mode requires TLS, a trusted certificate chain, and a certificate matching DB_HOST. Supported modes are disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca, and verify-full. Prefer verify-full in production. For an isolated localhost server without TLS only, explicitly use DB_SSLMODE=disable; do not weaken production TLS to fix a certificate problem. SQL Server's DB_ENCRYPT/DB_TRUST_SERVER_CERTIFICATE settings do not affect PostgreSQL.

    Connections use TCP with a hostname or IPv4 address, not Unix socket paths or arbitrary DSN fragments. Set DB_PORT=5432: the example file explicitly uses 3306 for MySQL. If the variable is entirely absent, the configured driver selects the appropriate default. Connection setup has a 15-second timeout, UTF-8 client encoding, and UTC session time zone. Database names accepted by this configuration are 1..63 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, dots, or hyphens, beginning with a letter, digit, or underscore.

    Terminal
    php osoni migrate
php osoni migrate:status
php osoni db:seed

    The migration runner uses same-named overrides in database/migrations/pgsql/ for the four shipped migrations. Existing top-level migration files and their history names are unchanged. Custom migrations must still have a top-level file; optionally supply a same-named PostgreSQL override or write driver-aware SQL. Do not edit applied migrations. Switching drivers does not transfer data.

    PostgreSQL migrations and bookkeeping run transactionally. A database-scoped session advisory lock prevents overlapping Osoni migration processes, in addition to the local file lock. Operations PostgreSQL prohibits inside a transaction (for example CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) cannot be used in normal migrations; plan those separately with appropriate operational safeguards.

    The query builder uses double-quoted simple identifiers, LIMIT/OFFSET, bound values, and INSERT ... RETURNING for generated keys. Custom incrementing and nonincrementing ORM keys work through the same APIs as the other databases. Use explicit stable ordering for pagination.

    PHP
    $id = $app->db->table('notes')->insert(['title' => 'A PostgreSQL note']);
$note = $app->db->table('notes')->findOrFail($id);
$page = $app->db->table('notes')->orderBy('id')->paginate(20, 1);

    Raw SQL passed to PDO or execute() is not translated. Use PostgreSQL SQL in custom migrations, seeders, and queries. Registration and IMAP deduplication use ON CONFLICT so expected duplicates do not abort surrounding transactions. PostgreSQL text cannot contain NUL bytes; encode binary application data or use an application-specific bytea binding path rather than storing it as text.

    PostgreSQL Validation

    The native suite includes recording-PDO PostgreSQL dialect tests. A separate live integration test checks schema/rollback, seeds, Unicode CRUD, ORM, pagination, transactions, duplicate registration, verification/password reset, API tokens, rate limits, email queue transitions, and duplicate IMAP imports without sending SMTP.

    Provision an empty, disposable database named osoni_test_*, then set these process environment variables in PowerShell, your Linux shell, or CI: PGSQL_TEST_DATABASE, PGSQL_TEST_HOST, PGSQL_TEST_PORT (default 5432), PGSQL_TEST_USERNAME, PGSQL_TEST_PASSWORD, and PGSQL_TEST_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=true. Optional PGSQL_TEST_SSLMODE defaults to verify-full; PGSQL_TEST_SSLROOTCERT supplies a CA file. Use disable only for an isolated local non-TLS test server. These variables are not read from .env.

    Terminal
    php tests/pgsql-integration.php

    The script refuses a nonempty database or a name outside osoni_test_*. It creates and removes framework tables. CI has a dedicated PostgreSQL 16 service job on Ubuntu with PHP 8.3/8.5; its local isolated connection disables TLS explicitly. A configured CI job is not proof of a successful run: validate your actual PostgreSQL/PHP/libpq/OS combination before deployment.

    Microsoft SQL Server

    SQL Server 2012+ syntax is supported through Microsoft's native PDO_SQLSRV PHP extension on Windows and Linux. Install a supported Microsoft ODBC Driver and a PDO_SQLSRV build matching your PHP version, architecture, and thread-safety mode. There is no Composer dependency. Check availability with:

    Terminal
    php -r "print_r(PDO::getAvailableDrivers());"

    The list must contain sqlsrv. Check the web server's PHP installation too. See Microsoft's PHP driver installation guide for platform prerequisites and supported PHP/driver versions. Do not assume every PDO_SQLSRV release supports every PHP release.

    Create the database and a dedicated SQL authentication login/user yourself. Select a least-privilege application account; migrations need additional DDL permissions and application-lock permission. Use the user's default schema consistently, normally dbo, for both web and CLI connections. Then update the existing settings in .env, without adding duplicate keys:

    DOTENV
    DB_CONNECTION=sqlsrv
DB_HOST=sql.example.test
DB_PORT=1433
DB_DATABASE=osoni
DB_USERNAME=osoni
DB_PASSWORD="your own password"
DB_ENCRYPT=true
DB_TRUST_SERVER_CERTIFICATE=false

    Use a hostname or IPv4 address and an explicit TCP port. Named instance suffixes, arbitrary DSN fragments, integrated Windows authentication, and Azure-specific authentication modes are not exposed by this configuration. When DB_PORT is absent it defaults to 1433 for sqlsrv, but the example file explicitly sets 3306 for MySQL: change that value when switching drivers. The connection has a 15-second login timeout.

    Encryption is enabled and certificate verification is required by default. Install a trusted server certificate whose name matches DB_HOST. DB_TRUST_SERVER_CERTIFICATE=true bypasses verification and should be restricted to isolated local testing, not used as a production certificate fix.

    Run the normal commands against the intended database:

    Terminal
    php osoni migrate
php osoni migrate:status
php osoni db:seed

    The migration runner selects same-named overrides in database/migrations/sqlsrv/ for the four shipped migrations. Original SQLite/MySQL migration files and migration history names remain unchanged. Custom migrations still live in database/migrations/; implement driver-aware SQL there, or provide a same-named SQL Server override. An override without a corresponding top-level migration is not discovered. Do not edit applied migrations; create new ones for subsequent schema changes. Switching drivers does not transfer an existing database or its data.

    SQL Server migrations use transactional DDL and a database application lock alongside the local file lock. The supplied schema uses BIGINT IDENTITY, NVARCHAR for Unicode text, DATETIME2 for note dates, and a filtered unique index so multiple outgoing emails can have a null IMAP source key. SQL Server TIMESTAMP is a rowversion, not a date/time column.

    The query builder uses square-bracket identifiers, TOP for limits and OFFSET/FETCH for paging. Use an explicit stable order for pagination. Inserts retrieve IDs with OUTPUT INSERTED, not session-wide @@IDENTITY. An incrementing model can declare a custom primary key; a nonincrementing model does not request an identity result.

    PHP
    $id = $app->db->table('notes')->insert(['title' => 'Unicode: café']);
$page = $app->db->table('notes')->orderBy('id')->paginate(20, 1);
// For a custom identity column:
$id = $app->db->table('articles')->insert(['title' => 'Hello'], identity: 'article_id');
// For a table without an identity result, insert() returns 0:
$app->db->table('settings')->insert(['code' => 'theme', 'value' => 'light'], identity: null);

    Raw SQL passed to execute() or PDO is not translated. Write T-SQL for raw queries, migrations, and seeders when this driver is selected. Driver-specific limits still apply, including SQL Server's 2100-parameter ceiling. The ID-returning insert path does not support enabled INSERT triggers on the target table; use an application-specific, audited OUTPUT INTO/stored-procedure path if such triggers are required.

    SQL Server Validation

    The standard native test suite includes recording-PDO SQL Server dialect tests; it does not connect to a real SQL Server. For a live run, provision an empty, disposable database whose name begins with osoni_test_. Set these process environment variables through PowerShell, your Linux shell, or CI: SQLSRV_TEST_DATABASE, SQLSRV_TEST_HOST, SQLSRV_TEST_PORT (default 1433), SQLSRV_TEST_USERNAME, SQLSRV_TEST_PASSWORD, and SQLSRV_TEST_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=true. Do not put real application credentials in the test configuration. These variables are read directly from the process, not from .env.

    Only for a local self-signed test server, set SQLSRV_TEST_TRUST_SERVER_CERTIFICATE=true. Encryption remains enabled. Run:

    Terminal
    php tests/sqlsrv-integration.php

    The script refuses a nonempty database or a name outside osoni_test_*. It creates and removes framework tables and checks migrations/rollback, repeatable seeds, Unicode CRUD, ORM, pagination, transactions, authentication, password reset, API tokens, rate limits, and database mail transitions. No SMTP connection is made. Run this against your supported SQL Server/PHP/ODBC combination before deployment; recording tests are not live compatibility proof.

    Native ORM and Query Builder

    The ORM consists of framework/Query.php and framework/Model.php, explicitly loaded in the bootstrap. Each query and model receives the existing Database instance. There are no packages, autoloading, global connections, schema inspection, or automatic migrations. The SQL is designed for SQLite, MySQL, SQL Server, and PostgreSQL; the existing cross-platform PDO configuration remains authoritative.

    Table Queries: Arrays

    PHP
    $query = $app->db->table('notes');
$id = $query->insert(['title' => 'My note']);
$note = $query->find($id);          // array of null
$note = $query->findOrFail($id);    // array of RecordNotFoundException

$recent = $query->where('id', '>', 0)
    ->where('title', 'LIKE', '%note%')
    ->orderBy('id', 'desc')
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

$query->where('id', $id)->update(['title' => 'Updated']); // row count
$query->where('id', $id)->delete();                       // row count

    Queries are immutable: where, orderBy, limit, and offset return a new query. Therefore, retain the result or chain the calls. All where conditions are combined with AND:

    PHP
    $query = $app->db->table('notes');
$filtered = $query->whereIn('id', [1, 2, 3])->whereNotNull('title');
$first = $filtered->first();            // array or null
$first = $filtered->firstOrFail();      // exception if absent
$count = $filtered->count();            // int
$exists = $filtered->exists();          // bool
$rows = $filtered->orderBy('id')->limit(10)->offset(10)->get();

    Supported operators: =, !=, <>, <, <=, >, >=, LIKE, NOT LIKE. where('column', $value) uses =. where('column', null) and where('column', '!=', null) use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, respectively; explicit whereNull/whereNotNull are also available. whereIn expects a list of up to 500 non-null values; an empty list finds or modifies no rows. LIKE wildcards % and _ retain their SQL meaning: parameter binding does not make them literal.

    Values are bound as int, bool, string, or null; floats are bound as textual numbers. Arrays, objects, resources, INF, and NAN are rejected. Table and column names must be simple identifiers (letters, digits, or underscores, not starting with a digit); they are quoted. Operators and sort directions are checked. The builder does not accept SQL fragments, joins, aliases, schema/table prefixes, OR groups, or raw expressions. For more complex SQL, intentionally use Database::execute() with bindings. Even with valid column names, choose yourself which ones a user may query or modify: identifier validation is not authorization.

    update and delete without an explicit WHERE are rejected. Writes with sorting, limits, or offsets are also rejected so conditions are never silently ignored. insert/create does not accept filters, sorting, or pagination. insert([]) uses database defaults and returns the PDO insert ID (int if representable, otherwise string); with manual keys, use the supplied key, not this driver-dependent ID. get() retrieves all matching rows unless you specify a limit. count() and exists() use the filters and ignore read limits, offsets, and sorting. offset with get() requires an explicit limit.

    Models: Objects

    Terminal
    php osoni make:model Article

    The generator creates a Model subclass with a snake_case name plus s as the default table name. There is intentionally no language-dependent pluralization: check the name, create the table through a migration, and populate $fillable. The default list is empty: no fields are mass assignable.

    Example for a custom articles table with the columns shown:

    PHP
    <?php
declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\Models;

final class Article extends \Osoni\Model
{
    protected string $table = 'articles';
    protected bool $timestamps = true;
    protected array $fillable = ['author_id', 'title', 'published', 'metadata', 'published_at'];
    protected array $hidden = ['metadata'];
    protected array $casts = [
        'id' => 'int',
        'author_id' => 'int',
        'published' => 'bool',
        'metadata' => 'json',
        'published_at' => 'datetime',
        'created_at' => 'datetime',
        'updated_at' => 'datetime',
    ];

    public function author(): \Osoni\Query
    {
        return $this->belongsTo(Author::class, 'author_id');
    }
}

    By default, a model has primary key id, $incrementing = true, and $timestamps = false. Enable timestamps only if both columns created_at and updated_at exist. Use UTC fields that can store values in Y-m-d H:i:s. Define foreign keys and database defaults explicitly in your migration. A model does not run schema migrations or content validation.

    PHP
    require_once $app->root . '/app/models/Article.php';
require_once $app->root . '/app/models/Author.php';

$articles = new \App\Models\Article($app->db);
$article = $articles->create([
    'author_id' => 1,
    'title' => 'My first article',
    'published' => false,
    'metadata' => ['tags' => ['php']],
    'published_at' => null,
]);

$article->title = 'A new title'; // checks fillable and cast
$changes = $article->dirty();        // changed fields in storage format
$article->save();                    // insert new model; otherwise changes only
$article->update(['published' => true]);
$article->refresh();                 // reload; overwrites local changes

$found = $articles->query()->findOrFail($article->id); // Article-object
$list = $articles->query()->where('published', true)->orderBy('id')->get();
$article->delete();                  // deletes the row; do not save again

    create() always creates a new model, even if you call it on a loaded record. query()->create() is an equivalent alternative. save(), update(), and delete() return true on success and explicitly fail on database errors. Reading an unknown/unloaded field throws a LogicException. exists() on a model returns the locally known saved state; for a current database check, use query()->where(...)->exists(). After a write, defaults and database values are reloaded. Saving an unchanged model writes nothing. refresh() or a write on a deleted row throws RecordNotFoundException; an unchanged save() does not check again. The central exception handler maps RecordNotFoundException to a generic HTTP 404 without exposing record identifiers. Catch it explicitly when your controller needs a different response.

    fill() and field assignment accept only $fillable. Unknown fields are not silently ignored. The primary key of a saved model and automatic timestamps are not writable. For manual/string keys, set $incrementing = false, choose $primaryKey, and add that key to $fillable for creation.

    Composite primary keys use a nonincrementing list of column names; every key column must be fillable for inserts:

    PHP
    final class TenantSetting extends \Osoni\Model
{
    protected string $table = 'tenant_settings';
    protected array $primaryKey = ['tenant_id', 'code'];
    protected bool $incrementing = false;
    protected array $fillable = ['tenant_id', 'code', 'value'];
}

$setting = (new TenantSetting($app->db))->query()->findOrFail([
    'tenant_id' => 7,
    'code' => 'locale',
]);

    Composite lookup arrays must name exactly the configured key columns, but may list them in any order. CRUD, refresh, delete, and default pagination ordering use every key column. keyNames() returns all key columns; keyName() remains available for a single-column key and throws for a composite key. Relationship key arguments may be lists paired by position when relating composite keys.

    Model queries also support filtered bulk update/delete. update checks fillable fields and casts, but works without model instances: automatic timestamps are not updated. Use save() or update() on a loaded model if you want that. Primary-key updates through a model query are always rejected. Model protections do not apply to a table query. insert() is only for table queries; use create() for model queries.

    Casts and Serialization

    CastPHP value on assignmentValue when read
    intintint, with overflow checking during hydration
    floatfinite int/floatfloat
    boolboolbool; stored as 0/1
    stringstringstring
    jsonarrayarray; JSON with explicit error messages
    datetimeDateTimeInterfaceDateTimeImmutable in UTC
    encryptedstringdecrypted string
    encrypted:jsonarraydecrypted array

    Null remains null for all casts; the database determines whether a column allows null. Without a cast, only scalars/null are allowed and PDO values are used.
