Casts are intentionally strict on assignment: form text 'false', for example, does not accidentally become true. Validate and convert form input yourself. Dates use UTC with second precision. On SQL Server, hydration also accepts a DATETIME2 fractional suffix of one to seven zeros; nonzero fractions are rejected rather than discarded. Other drivers require the second-precision format. JSON objects become associative arrays when read; update a JSON field by assigning the modified array again, not by indirectly mutating an array on a magic property. Invalid JSON, dates, or other invalid stored values throw an exception.

    PHP
    $array = $article->toArray();
$json = json_encode($article, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);

    $hidden excludes fields from toArray() and JSON, including within a list or pagination. For a user model, for example, put password_hash in $hidden and also exclude it from $fillable if it should not be mass assignable. Hidden fields remain directly readable by your own PHP code; the database and dirty() also contain hidden values. Dates are returned in arrays/JSON as UTC ISO-8601 strings. Serialization does not run relationship queries. The existing authentication intentionally uses its own atomic SQL for tokens, queues, and session versions; it does not need to be rewritten for this.

    Relationships

    Define relationships with explicit model classes and keys. The related class must itself be loaded through require_once:

    PHP
    final class Author extends \Osoni\Model
{
    protected string $table = 'authors';
    protected array $fillable = ['name'];

    public function articles(): \Osoni\Query
    {
        return $this->hasMany(Article::class, 'author_id');
    }
}

$author = $article->author()->first(); // Author of null
$authorArticles = $author->articles()->where('published', true)->get();

    hasMany(Related::class, foreignKey, localKey) uses the model's primary key as localKey by default. belongsTo(Related::class, foreignKey, ownerKey) uses the related model's primary key by default. For composite-key relationships, pass lists of corresponding foreign/local or foreign/owner columns in the same order. Both return a new, filterable model query on the same database connection. A null relationship key returns no results. Relationships on unsaved models are rejected; records are not automatically saved or associated. For a nullable belongsTo, check for null yourself before navigating further.

    There is no implicit lazy loading through properties, eager loading, relationship cache, cascade-save, polymorphism, or many-to-many API. Relationship queries inside a loop therefore run as separate queries; for larger lists, deliberately fetch the required rows in batches with whereIn. Cascades and referential integrity belong in your migrations.

    Pagination and Transactions

    PHP
    $page = $articles->query()->orderBy('id', 'desc')->paginate(20, 2);
// [
//   'data' => [Article, ...],
//   'total' => 42,
//   'per_page' => 20,
//   'current_page' => 2,
//   'last_page' => 3,
// ]

    Table queries return the same shape with arrays in data. Page numbers are positive; page size is 1 to 100. Without explicit sorting, the primary key is used (id for table queries). When sorting by custom fields, also sort by a unique key for stable pages. An empty dataset has last_page = 1; pages beyond the end have empty data. Counting and retrieval are separate queries, not a snapshot during concurrent changes.

    PHP
    $app->db->transaction(function () use ($app): void {
    $authors = new \App\Models\Author($app->db);
    $authors->create(['name' => 'Ada']);
    // Other database writes on the same connection.
});

    Model writes use the same PDO connection and participate in the existing transaction. Nested transactions, optimistic locking, soft deletes, and model events have not been added. After rollback, use new/reloaded instances: a rollback restores the database, not previously changed PHP objects. The ORM does not replace validation, route guards, or per-record authorization.

    For a transaction-scoped row lock, use lockForUpdate() on a row-returning query inside Database::transaction(). MySQL and PostgreSQL use FOR UPDATE; SQL Server uses UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK hints. Calling it outside a transaction or on SQLite throws explicitly. Locks remain subject to the database engine's isolation level and lock-escalation behavior.

    PHP
    $app->db->transaction(function () use ($app, $id): void {
    $job = $app->db->table('background_jobs')
        ->where('id', $id)
        ->lockForUpdate()
        ->firstOrFail();
    // Validate the locked state and perform related writes here.
});

    Encryption

    The native Encryption service uses AES-256-GCM through OpenSSL: 256-bit keys, a new cryptographically random 12-byte nonce per encryption, and a full 16-byte authentication tag. Data is returned only if the integrity check succeeds. There is no fallback to plaintext, a default key, or insecure encryption.

    Creating and Storing a Key

    Terminal
    php osoni key:generate

    This displays one APP_KEY=base64:... line. Copy it to your local .env or set APP_KEY through your deployment's environment configuration/secret store. The command changes no files and never overwrites an existing key. Each execution displays a new key; do not casually replace a key that already protects data. --force is not accepted. Run the command in a private terminal, not in shared CI logs.

    The key must contain exactly 32 random bytes, canonically base64-encoded with the base64: prefix; a password or custom text key is rejected. No key is automatically generated at boot or per request. Without APP_KEY, the framework continues to work until you use encryption, a non-null encrypted cast, or authenticator MFA enrollment/verification; then an explicit EncryptionException is thrown.

    Store a secure key backup separately from the database. Share the same key with the web app, CLI, and workers that must decrypt the same data; use different keys for different applications/environments. Never commit real keys. Protect .env, environment variables, server logs, and backups; do not dump the application configuration. Encrypted data cannot be recovered without the original key.

    Using the Service

    PHP
    $encrypted = $app->encryption->encrypt('Confidential text', 'orders:notes');
$plaintext = $app->encryption->decrypt($encrypted, 'orders:notes');

    The optional context is authenticated but not stored in the payload. You must use exactly the same context to decrypt. Choose a fixed, application-specific context to prevent accidental reuse elsewhere. Empty strings, Unicode, and binary strings are supported. The output format is osoni:v1: followed by base64 of the nonce, tag, and ciphertext. The prefix/version and context are included as additional authenticated data. Encrypt the same value again and you get a different payload. The format does not use PHP serialization.

    PHP
    use Osoni\Encryption;

$encryption = new Encryption($configuredKey);
$encrypted = $encryption->encrypt($value);
$value = $encryption->decrypt($encrypted);

    Invalid/outdated payload formats, truncated or modified data, or an incorrect key or context throw Osoni\EncryptionException. A genuine operational failure must remain visible; do not catch it and then return empty text or the original ciphertext as if decryption succeeded. Errors contain no key or plaintext. Key and plaintext parameters are marked with SensitiveParameter; the service redacts key data in var_dump and cannot be serialized. This does not replace careful logging practices: your own code can still leak decrypted data.

    Encrypted ORM Casts

    PHP
    final class Customer extends \Osoni\Model
{
    protected string $table = 'customers';
    protected array $fillable = ['name', 'private_note', 'preferences'];
    protected array $hidden = ['private_note', 'preferences'];
    protected array $casts = [
        'private_note' => 'encrypted',
        'preferences' => 'encrypted:json',
    ];
}

$customers = new Customer($app->db);
$customer = $customers->create([
    'name' => 'Example',
    'private_note' => 'For internal use only',
    'preferences' => ['language' => 'en'],
]);
$text = $customer->private_note;       // decrypted string
$preferences = $customer->preferences; // decrypted array
$customer->update(['private_note' => 'New text']);

    encrypted accepts strings; encrypted:json accepts arrays. Both preserve null as database NULL. Bulk updates through a model query also use these casts. Hydration/refresh validates ciphertext without re-encrypting: unchanged data is not marked dirty and does not change during another field update. Assigning the same decrypted value again preserves the existing ciphertext. Deliberately assign new content if you want to replace it.

    Use TEXT or, for large payloads, MySQL LONGTEXT, not the original short VARCHAR: encryption adds 28 bytes and a prefix, and base64 further increases the payload. The exact storage length is 11 + 4 * ceil((28 + bytes) / 3). No existing columns or data are modified automatically.

    The ORM context contains the table name, column name, and cast type. Moving ciphertext to another table/column or changing the cast type is therefore rejected. The context does not contain a row ID: moving data between rows in the same column or restoring older valid data is not prevented. Encryption does not protect against replay, deletion, a compromised application, or an attacker with access to both data and key.

    Encryption does not automatically hide fields. Reading and toArray()/JSON return plaintext unless you add the field to $hidden. dirty() and direct $app->db->table(...) queries use the storage format. Table queries and handwritten SQL do not apply encrypted casts: use models when writing to encrypted columns.

    Because ciphertext is random, comparisons, whereIn with values, LIKE, sorting, and relationship keys on encrypted model fields are unusable; the model query explicitly rejects them. whereNull/whereNotNull and an empty whereIn remain usable. Primary keys and automatic timestamp columns must not have an encrypted cast. Also do not use a foreign/unique index as a logical plaintext comparison. Existing login email addresses, password hashes, reset/verification token hashes, and mail queue remain intentionally unchanged. Passwords remain one-way hashed, not reversibly encrypted.

    For a custom database instance, explicitly pass the same service:

    PHP
    $db = new \Osoni\Database($root, $databaseConfig, $encryption);

    Existing Data and Key Rotation

    Adding an encrypted cast to an existing plaintext column does not migrate anything: reading then intentionally fails. Create your own controlled migration to sufficiently large columns and encrypt existing values with the correct context. Back up first and test on a copy. Renaming a table/column also requires decrypting with the old context and encrypting with the new context.

    There is no automatic key rotation, keyring, or migration command. For a controlled rotation, stop all writers/workers, safely store the old key, decrypt with the old service, and encrypt with the new service using the same context. Verify all records/backups, switch all processes to the new key, and only then resume writes. Replacing APP_KEY alone makes previously encrypted data unreadable.

    Migrations and Seeds

    Terminal
    php osoni make:migration create_messages
php osoni make:migration:import import_legacy_schema
php osoni migrate
php osoni migrate:status
php osoni migrate:rollback
php osoni make:seeder MessageSeeder
php osoni db:seed MessageSeeder

    Fill in the generated up(PDO $db) and down(PDO $db) first. The templates intentionally throw an exception until implemented: this prevents an empty migration from being incorrectly recorded as run. make:migration:import instead captures the configured database's table definitions, indexes, keys, and constraints (not row data), excluding Osoni's migrations ledger. It reads but does not change the source database. Review the generated, driver-specific DDL; it is intended for a fresh database using the same driver and schema setup, not to be applied back to the source. Files are sorted by timestamp. Each run forms a batch; rollback reverses the entire last batch. Do not modify or delete applied migrations; create a new migration.

    SQLite, SQL Server, and PostgreSQL run each migration and its registration in a single transaction. MySQL DDL causes implicit commits: a failed migration may already be partially applied. Back up before changes and deliberately recover a partial migration before running again. Write driver-dependent SQL where needed; the example migration demonstrates this.

    A local file lock prevents concurrent migrations from the same project directory. MySQL, SQL Server, and PostgreSQL also use a database-wide advisory lock between Osoni processes. Use SQLite on a single host with local storage.

    Seeders return a Closure(PDO $db): void and run in a transaction. Use seeders for DML, not DDL. The example seeder is repeatable; ensure your own seeders are as well. Seeders are not registered as migrations.

    Database changes in production require --force:

    Terminal
    php osoni migrate --force
php osoni db:seed --force
php osoni migrate:rollback --force

    Generators refuse to overwrite existing files. New controllers and models are never loaded automatically.

    Email: SMTP, IMAP, and Database Queue

    This uses native PHP streams, OpenSSL for TLS, and iconv for incoming MIME headers and character sets. The IMAP extension, Composer, and mail() are not required. First configure your mail server and run the new migration:

    Terminal
    php osoni migrate

    In production, as usual, use php osoni migrate --force. An existing .env is not automatically updated. Add the following settings yourself; the full list is in .env.example.

    DOTENV
    MAIL_LOG=true
MAIL_FROM=sender@yourdomain.com
SMTP_HOST=smtp.yourprovider.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_ENCRYPTION=starttls
SMTP_USERNAME=sender@yourdomain.com
SMTP_PASSWORD="your app password"
IMAP_HOST=imap.yourprovider.com
IMAP_PORT=993
IMAP_ENCRYPTION=tls
IMAP_USERNAME=sender@yourdomain.com
IMAP_PASSWORD="your app password"
IMAP_MAILBOX=INBOX

    Use your provider's actual values; the hosts above are examples. SMTP and IMAP can use different accounts. Native password login is supported: SMTP AUTH PLAIN/LOGIN and IMAP LOGIN. Use an app password if needed. OAuth2 and providers that allow only OAuth2 are not supported.

    tls is direct TLS (commonly SMTP 465 and IMAP 993); starttls performs a required TLS upgrade (commonly SMTP 587 and IMAP 143). There is no fallback to unencrypted traffic. TLS 1.2+ with certificate and hostname verification is required for external servers. For a custom CA, set SMTP_CA_FILE and IMAP_CA_FILE to readable CA files; this does not disable verification. none is allowed only on localhost/127.0.0.1, without credentials, for example, for a local SMTP test server. IMAP then requires PREAUTH. SMTP_TIMEOUT and IMAP_TIMEOUT are socket timeouts of 1–300 seconds, 15 by default. Hosts are DNS names or IPv4 addresses, not URLs.

    Sending or Queuing from PHP

    Through $app in routes, or $this->app in controllers:

    PHP
    $message = $app->mail->compose([
    'to' => ['recipient@example.com'],
    'subject' => 'Welcome',
    'text' => 'Welcome to our application.',
    'html' => '<p>Welcome to our application.</p>',
]);

$id = $app->mail->send($message);   // Send immediately through SMTP.
// OR:
$id = $app->mail->queue($message);  // Store only; send later through the CLI.

    from is optional in compose() and defaults to MAIL_FROM. You can also directly use new \Osoni\Mail\Message(...). Use bare ASCII email addresses without display names; up to 100 recipients. Subjects and bodies are UTF-8. You can provide text, HTML, or both; providing both creates a multipart/alternative message. Subjects must not contain control characters and are limited to 500 bytes; bodies are limited to 5 MiB total. Headers are encoded and MIME bodies are base64-encoded. Cc, Bcc, attachments, and supplied headers are not included.

    MAIL_LOG=true is the default:

    • Directly sent outgoing messages are stored in emails before SMTP. The table stores the sender, recipients, subject, text, HTML, Message-ID, status, attempts, timestamps, and a sanitized error message.
    • A database error before sending prevents the message from being sent

    without a log. An SMTP error throws an exception and remains in the table.

    • Retrieved incoming messages are stored in the same table.
    • With logging enabled, send() returns the ID; otherwise, it returns null.

    With MAIL_LOG=false, direct sending and IMAP retrieval do not use an email table. **Explicitly using queue() or mail:queue always stores a message**: a database queue cannot operate without storage. All stored outgoing messages can still be sent through the CLI, and their status is updated. Settings and passwords are not stored in the email table.

    Sending Through the CLI

    Create a JSON file yourself, for example message.json:

    JSON
    {
  "to": ["recipient@example.com"],
  "subject": "Welcome",
  "text": "Welcome to our application.",
  "html": "<p>Welcome to our application.</p>"
}
    Terminal
    php osoni mail:queue /path/to/message.json
php osoni mail:list
php osoni mail:show 1
php osoni mail:send 1
php osoni mail:work 50

    mail:queue displays the new ID; replace 1 with that ID. The JSON file may be up to 6 MiB; the body content limit remains 5 MiB. Store such files outside public/ and do not commit confidential messages. mail:work processes one batch, oldest first, and stops at the first error with exit code 1. It is not a background daemon. You can run this command periodically through cron (Linux) or Task Scheduler (Windows), using absolute paths to PHP and osoni. mail:list, mail:show, and mail:fetch output JSON, so even untrusted subjects cannot execute terminal control codes.

    Delivery statuses:

    StatusMeaning
    queuedReady to send; the worker selects only this status.
    sendingAtomically claimed by a sending process.
    sentSMTP returned a 250 confirmation after DATA; delivery is not guaranteed.
    failedNot sent or explicitly rejected by SMTP.
    uncertainConnection lost after DATA began; SMTP may already have accepted the email.
    receivedRetrieved through IMAP; never directly sendable.
    Terminal
    php osoni mail:retry 1
php osoni mail:send 1

    mail:retry changes only failed back to queued. sent and incoming emails cannot be resent with these commands. Create a new message for an intentional resend. If a process crashes, the status may remain sending. In that case, first check the SMTP server and stop active workers; only then deliberately use mail:retry ID --force for sending or uncertain. This can cause duplicate delivery. There is intentionally no automatic timeout retry. The Message-ID remains the same on retries, but that does not guarantee recipient-side deduplication.

    If SMTP accepts the email but saving sent fails, the status remains sending and the caller receives an error. In that case, also check the SMTP server first. Concurrent workers can never claim the same queued row; if a claim conflict occurs, the worker stops explicitly and the next scheduled run can proceed. SMTP acceptance is not the same as delivery: bounces are not processed automatically. Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC at the domain/mail server level.

    Reading and Logging the IMAP Inbox

    Terminal
    php osoni mail:fetch 50

    Or from PHP:

    PHP
    $messages = $app->mail->fetch(50);
foreach ($messages as $message) {
    $id = $message['id'];            // null when MAIL_LOG=false
    $subject = $message['message']['subject'];
    $text = $message['message']['text'];
}

    The client opens the mailbox with EXAMINE and reads BODY.PEEK[]: messages are not marked as read, deleted, or moved. The default is INBOX; other mailbox names are ASCII or pre-encoded IMAP modified UTF-7. When logging is enabled, the oldest UIDs not yet stored are retrieved so repeated batches work through the inbox. Without logging, the most recent UIDs are retrieved and there is no persistent import checkpoint. Limits are 1–1000 messages per run, 50 by default.

    Deduplication uses server, port, account, mailbox, UIDVALIDITY, and UID; the unique database index also protects concurrent imports. A changed UIDVALIDITY or account/server configuration can intentionally cause a new import. Deleted database rows can be imported again. The server is queried with UID SEARCH ALL on each run; metadata is limited to 2 MiB per response.

    Incoming MIME is parsed into text and HTML, including base64, quoted-printable, RFC 2047 headers, and iconv character sets. Attachments are not unpacked; the exact original email remains base64-encoded in raw_message. headers_json stores the original unfolded headers; outgoing emails store structured fields instead of a raw copy. Incoming to_addresses contains the original To header as a single list item, not a validated recipient list. Incoming data is never reused as an outgoing Message.

    The default maximum is 10 MiB raw per message (IMAP_MAX_BYTES), configurable up to 50 MiB; each batch is limited to 50 MiB raw. MIME nesting is limited to 10 and the number of parts to 100. Larger, malformed, or unsupported messages cause an explicit error, not an apparently successful import. A parse/network error during retrieval does not save that batch. If a later database error occurs, earlier inserts in the batch may be retained; deduplication makes the next run safe.

    Protect access to emails, backups, and the CLI: messages may contain confidential data. Base64 is not encryption. Set your own retention period, restricted database permissions, and appropriate storage security. Incoming HTML is not sanitized: never render it directly in your application; display it as text with e() or use a separate, well-sanitized and protected viewer.

    Configuration

    System environment variables take precedence over .env. .env supports NAME=value, optional single/double quotes, and full-line comments. There is no interpolation, escape processing, multiline, or inline comment syntax. Use true/false for booleans. .env and database files are in .gitignore; new .env and SQLite files get Linux permissions 0600. On Windows, the folder's NTFS ACLs apply; restrict them in advance. APP_ENV accepts only local, testing, and production; a typo therefore does not silently disable production security.

    Production and Security Boundaries

    Deployment checks and readiness

    The framework provides production safeguards, not automatic production configuration. Local .env values are intentionally preserved during upgrades. Run these commands as the deployment/service identity after configuring the environment and before routing traffic to the new release:

    Terminal
    php osoni storage:prepare
php osoni migrate --force
php osoni doctor

    Back up the database first and use backward-compatible migrations during rolling releases. storage:prepare creates the private storage root and its logs, uploads, and views children, plus files for local file storage. It does not provision remote buckets/containers, move files, adjust existing ownership, configure sessions, or change database contents.

    doctor prints PASS, WARN, or FAIL for production flags, trusted HTTPS origin, extensions, private storage, database/schema/migration readiness, encryption, mail configuration, and operational concerns. Its exit code is 1 when any check fails and 0 otherwise; review warnings too. It does not create directories, databases, migration tables, or records, send email, or call AI. An SMTP configuration warning is not evidence that real mail delivery works. It checks the CLI PHP installation; verify the web/FPM installation separately. If bootstrap configuration is invalid, the command exits with the normal startup error before diagnostics can run.

    WARN mfa-enforcement is an explicit EMERGENCY warning when password and OIDC MFA challenges are bypassed. Restore AUTH_MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=true and restart all application processes after the emergency. The warning does not revoke sessions: those created during the bypass remain authorized until expiry or explicit revocation. A warning alone does not change the command's exit code.

    • GET /health: lightweight process liveness only; a 200 does not prove that the database is usable.
    • GET /ready: 200 with {"status":"ready"} only when private storage exists and is readable/writable, the existing database accepts reads, bundled tables exist, and applied migration names match the deployed files. Otherwise it returns 503 with {"status":"not_ready"} and logs safe failure metadata. It never creates a missing SQLite database or runs migrations.
    • Exact GET/HEAD requests to those two probe paths do not start a session or issue a session cookie. HEAD responses have an empty body.

    Restrict probes to your load balancer/monitoring network at the web server. Readiness performs database reads, so set a sensible polling interval and edge rate limits. It does not test SMTP/AI availability, usable free disk space, backup recovery, real writes, or application-specific dependencies. Database network/query deadlines must also be set in the database/server/PHP stack. The framework retains provider/driver-specific timeout behavior rather than claiming a universal probe deadline.

    Persistent storage across releases

    DOTENV
    STORAGE_PATH=/srv/osoni-data

    On Windows, use an absolute native path such as C:/OsoniData. Default storage remains project-relative. The configured location contains private logs/, uploads/, views/, and migrations.lock; $app->storagePath exposes the resolved path. The default configured services and CLI use this location. Standalone Logger/Uploads/Migrator constructors accept an optional storagePath; standalone custom View caches remain caller-managed.

    Set a real directory, not a symlink. Public paths, ancestors of public/, dot segments (./..), stream wrappers, and symlink ancestors are rejected. Configure an absolute shared data directory directly rather than symlinking each release's storage/. Keep the code read-only for the web identity. Existing directories are not chmodded or chowned by storage:prepare; restrict POSIX permissions or inherited NTFS ACLs explicitly.

    Changing STORAGE_PATH does not move existing data. Stop or drain writers, back up and copy uploads and required logs to the new private directory, preserve ownership/ACLs, deploy consistent settings to web and workers, and verify downloads before switching traffic. Compiled views may be regenerated. Do not run view:clear against a cache actively used by other releases; prefer leaving content-addressed cache entries until old workers have drained.

    SQLite is independent: set DB_DATABASE to an absolute persistent file path outside the release and public directories. Do not copy a live SQLite database as an ordinary file without a consistent backup procedure. PHP session storage is also independent: configure the web SAPI's session.save_handler and session.save_path, permissions, and retention. Multiple nodes need shared sessions or appropriate sticky routing and common upload storage. SQLite on network filesystems is not supported.

    MySQL TLS configuration

    MySQL TLS is optional. Select a mode in .env; the default is disabled in every environment, including production:

    DOTENV
    DB_MYSQL_TLS=disabled

    This creates a normal MySQL connection without SSL/TLS PDO options. Osoni does not require a CA, restrict the host, or override DB_HOST. The MySQL client/server configuration may still impose its own transport requirements.

    To require encryption without certificate verification:

    DOTENV
    DB_MYSQL_TLS=required

    To require encryption and verify the server certificate with a CA:

    DOTENV
    DB_MYSQL_TLS=verify_ca
DB_MYSQL_SSL_CA=/absolute/path/to/ca.pem

    The CA must exist as a readable local file, not a directory; use an absolute path. Native PDO verifies the certificate, which should match DB_HOST. Windows paths can use forward slashes, for example C:/certs/mysql-ca.pem. Both enabled modes reject connections without a negotiated TLS cipher; Osoni does not retry in plaintext.

    For backward compatibility, existing DB_MYSQL_TLS=required configurations with DB_MYSQL_SSL_CA continue to verify the server certificate. An invalid configured CA remains an error in either enabled mode. Applications that previously relied on the implicit TLS default must explicitly select required or verify_ca to retain TLS.

    DB_HOST is always respected, including localhost. On systems where localhost selects a Unix socket, an enabled TLS mode fails if TLS is not negotiated; choose a TCP host explicitly when your deployment needs it. Programmatic Database settings use tls and ssl_ca with the same modes and default. PostgreSQL and SQL Server keep their existing TLS settings.

    Request limits and reverse proxies

    Every application/json request, including non-API routes, now has a fixed 1 MiB raw-body cap. All API bodies retain that cap. Bounded reads enforce it even without Content-Length; oversized input returns 413. This is separate from the 2 MiB per-upload default: set PHP/web-server multipart limits with appropriate overhead. Edge limits must reject oversized traffic before it reaches PHP, which may parse some request types first.

    Client identity still uses REMOTE_ADDR, never arbitrary forwarded headers. Configure Apache mod_remoteip or Nginx real_ip using only your trusted proxy CIDRs, and block direct traffic bypassing the proxy. Otherwise clients behind that proxy share application rate limits. TLS termination also needs SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true and HTTPS redirection/HSTS at the edge.

    Operations and release gate

    1. Use APP_ENV=production, APP_DEBUG=false, a real HTTPS APP_URL, and a valid application key before using encryption. Keep the key backed up separately from encrypted data. Disable or edge-protect API documentation.
    2. Verify sender authorization and real SMTP delivery in staging. Run php osoni mail:work 50 periodically with cron/systemd timers on Linux or Task Scheduler on Windows. The command processes one batch and exits; it is not a permanent worker. Prevent overlapping runs, alert on nonzero exits, and monitor queued age plus failed/uncertain/sending states. Recover uncertain mail manually to avoid duplicate delivery; never blindly force retries.
    3. Keep consistent backups of the database, private uploads, and encryption keys. Perform and document a restore rehearsal on an isolated environment; verify ownership, downloads, account recovery, and encrypted records.
    4. Monitor 5xx/503 responses, request latency, disk space, log write failures, queue backlog, certificate expiration, and database connection saturation. Export operational logs if the default five-day local retention is too short.
    5. Test the actual PHP-FPM/Apache/IIS configuration and selected database, enforce application/per-record authorization, and load-test expected traffic. Set realistic process, socket, request-body, AI, and proxy timeouts.

    The CI definition includes native Ubuntu/Windows tests and separate PostgreSQL and MySQL integration jobs. SQL Server still requires its opt-in live test on a suitable server. CI definitions are not proof that the jobs have executed successfully: require green results and your staging/recovery checks before release.

    For a disposable empty MySQL database named osoni_test_*, set process variables MYSQL_TEST_DATABASE, MYSQL_TEST_HOST, MYSQL_TEST_PORT, MYSQL_TEST_USERNAME, MYSQL_TEST_PASSWORD, MYSQL_TEST_TLS, MYSQL_TEST_SSL_CA, and MYSQL_TEST_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=true, then run:

    Terminal
    php tests/mysql-integration.php

    These settings are process environment variables, not .env values. TLS defaults to required; disabled is only for a local disposable test server. The script checks emptiness, creates/test-drops its schema, and sends no SMTP.

    • Set the document root **only to public/**, never to the project root.
    • Use HTTPS, APP_ENV=production, and APP_DEBUG=false.
    • Behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, set SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true. The framework intentionally does not automatically trust forwarded headers.
    • Production refuses to start without HTTPS or explicit secure-cookie configuration. A secure cookie does not encrypt an HTTP connection: also enforce HTTPS in your web server or proxy.
    • Ensure PHP errors go only to protected server logs; also configure PHP itself with display_errors=Off and log_errors=On.
    • Give only the required user write access to the SQLite database, database directory, and storage/. On Linux, a file created with 0600 is readable only by its owner: align the CLI/PHP-FPM user accordingly. On Windows, restrict NTFS ACLs to the required users. Do not make the entire application writable by the web server.
    • Limit request sizes and timeouts in PHP and the web server; configure rate limiting and TLS/HSTS at the proxy or web server level.
    • Default headers include CSP, nosniff, frame blocking, a restricted permissions policy, and Cache-Control: no-store for application responses. The default CSP allows no scripts or inline styles; only the Swagger documentation gets the limited exception described above. Custom responses can explicitly change headers; keep such changes limited.
    • Static files are served directly by the web server: configure suitable caching and security headers for them yourself.
    • Protect custom routes with the auth guard and add per-object authorization and application-specific validation before public use.
    • Never run the development server as a production server. Security measures are not a guarantee: have a real application reviewed before deployment.

    Use the maintained Web Server Deployment templates for Apache, Nginx, FrankenPHP, or IIS rather than ad hoc rewrite rules. Configure HTTPS for the actual service. Never put confidential files or uploads containing executable code in public/.

    Native Scheduling and Background Jobs

    Osoni's scheduler decides when work runs inside a long-running PHP process. It does not need cron or Windows Task Scheduler. Durable jobs use the application database, not Redis, Composer packages, or serialized PHP objects.

    Quick Start

    Configure the application's existing database first. Then run:

    Terminal
    php osoni scheduler:install
php osoni migrate

    The install command checks prerequisites and explains setup; it does not change your database or overwrite application files. In production, review and back up the database before running php osoni migrate --force.

    Define tasks in routes/schedule.php, which returns a registration callback:

    PHP
    use Osoni\Application;
use Osoni\Scheduler\Schedule;

return static function (Schedule $schedule, Application $app): void {
    $schedule->command('mail:work', ['50'])
        ->everyMinute()
        ->withoutOverlapping();
};

    Start the scheduler in a dedicated terminal:

    Terminal
    php osoni scheduler:work

    The command stays running; this is expected. Use another terminal for your web server. php osoni scheduler:work is an alias for the same CLI. Direct scheduled tasks use the default queue unless explicitly changed; changing QUEUE_DEFAULT only changes the ordinary queue worker's default selection, not the scheduler's.

    For schedules using ->queue('billing'), also start a queue worker:

    Terminal
    php osoni queue:work --queue=billing

    Defining Tasks and Frequencies

    Application handlers are trusted code. Explicitly require their PHP files in the registration file; Osoni does not discover or autoload classes.

    PHP
    $schedule->task('cleanup')
    ->everyMinutes(5)
    ->run(static function (): void {
        CleanupService::run();
    });

$schedule->task('invoice-processing')
    ->dailyAt('02:00')
    ->timezone('Europe/Amsterdam')
    ->withoutOverlapping()
    ->runMissed(limit: 1)
    ->retries(3)
    ->retryAfter(60)
    ->timeout(600)
    ->queue('billing')
    ->run([InvoiceService::class, 'process']);

    Frequencies include everySecond(), everySeconds(10), everyMinute(), everyMinutes(5), hourly(), everyHours(2), daily(), dailyAt('02:00'), weekly(), weeklyOn(1, '08:00'), and monthly(). Weekly days use ISO numbering: Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7. Monthly means the first day of the month at midnight. Interval schedules use a stable UTC anchor; calendar schedules use the task's timezone.

    Use unique, stable task names. Do not rename a task or change a pending job's handler without reviewing persisted work. Definition fingerprints protect against silently running queued occurrences with incompatible definitions.

    Registered Jobs and JSON Payloads

    routes/jobs.php returns explicitly registered job types. Validators reject bad payloads before dispatch and again before execution:

    PHP
    return [
    'invoice.generate.v1' => [
        'validate' => static function (array $payload): void {
            if (array_keys($payload) !== ['invoice_id']
                || !is_int($payload['invoice_id']) || $payload['invoice_id'] < 1) {
                throw new InvalidArgumentException('A positive invoice_id is required.');
            }
        },
        'handle' => static function (
            array $payload,
            \Osoni\Queue\ExecutionContext $context,
        ) use ($app): void {
            $context->checkpoint();
            // Require InvoiceService explicitly in this registry before use.
            InvoiceService::generate($payload['invoice_id'], $context->idempotencyKey());
        },
    ],
];

    Queue a job through the application service:

    PHP
    $id = $app->queue->dispatch(
    'invoice.generate.v1',
    ['invoice_id' => 123],
    queue: 'billing',
    priority: 2,
    tries: 3,
    backoff: [60, 300],
    timeout: 300,
    unique: 'invoice:123',
);

    Payloads are bounded JSON data, not executable code. Do not put credentials, large documents, or unnecessary personal data in them; store a record ID and retrieve authorized data in the handler. Queue database access is privileged. Never expose dispatch, retry, or monitoring services as unauthenticated routes.

    runNow($type, $payload) invokes a registered handler in the caller. It is synchronous and does not provide durable delivery, process isolation, or worker recovery. Prefer dispatch() for background work.

    For bounded exponential delays, use \Osoni\Queue\Queue::exponentialBackoff(30, 2, 300) as the backoff argument. This returns [30, 60], suitable for the two retries of a three-attempt job. Unique dispatch keys deduplicate active work of the same registered job type.

    Claims, Overlaps, and Multiple Servers

    Each scheduled occurrence has one database identity. Atomic conditional claims ensure only one worker owns that occurrence at a time. Every completion checks the claim credential; a stale worker cannot acknowledge a newer claim.

    withoutOverlapping() additionally excludes simultaneous execution of different occurrences of the same task. It coalesces missed work into at most one latest occurrence and suppresses new occurrences while any earlier one is pending, reserved, running, or uncertain. onOneServer() explicitly declares the existing cluster-wide occurrence guarantee; omitting it does not cause one execution per server.

    All cooperating nodes must share the same application database, synchronize their system clocks, and deploy compatible handler registrations. SQLite is for local/single-host operation, not independent database files on multiple servers or a shared network drive.

    The bundled background-work migration separates definition/runtime/history:

    TableResponsibility
    osoni_scheduler_tasksDefinition fingerprint and durable schedule cursor
    scheduled_occurrencesUnique task/time occurrence identity, retained after job-history pruning
    background_jobsRegistered job type, JSON payload, queue, retry policy, ownership, and current state
    background_attemptsIndividual execution attempts and safe outcome metadata
    background_workersWorker identity, heartbeat, stop request, and state
    background_locksUniqueness and overlap ownership

    This uses one additional table compared with keeping occurrence uniqueness only on job rows: retained occurrence tombstones prevent history pruning from accidentally allowing an old occurrence to be created again. Schedule handlers remain in application code, never in these tables.

    Retries, Failure, and Crash Recovery

    retries(3) means three additional scheduled attempts, or four total. Scheduled tasks default to zero additional retries and a 300-second timeout. Queue tries: 3 and worker --tries=3 mean three total attempts. Backoff controls when a failed attempt becomes eligible again. A job exception does not stop the whole worker.

    Use Osoni\Queue\RetryableJobFailure to declare a known retryable failure, or Osoni\Queue\JobFailure to declare a known terminal failure. Unexpected exceptions are treated conservatively because earlier side effects may already have happened. For an idempotent job that may safely repeat, explicitly pass retrySafe: true when dispatching, or use ->retrySafe() on a scheduled task. This is an application assertion, not an automatic proof of idempotency.

    States distinguish pending, reserved, running, completed, failed, and uncertain work. If application work succeeds but its acknowledgement is lost, Osoni cannot know whether it is safe to repeat that work. An expired heartbeat is not proof that the old PHP process stopped.

    Do not assume exactly-once execution. Use stable idempotency keys and unique business constraints. For external APIs, pass their supported idempotency key. For atomic application updates plus enqueueing, dispatch on the same connection inside your database transaction; Osoni does not commit the caller's transaction. External effects require application-specific outbox/idempotency handling.

    Terminal
    php osoni queue:failed
php osoni queue:retry JOB_ID
php osoni queue:retry-all

    Retry-all processes at most 100 confirmed failures per call and excludes uncertain work. Production retries require --force.

    For uncertain work, first investigate external effects and stop/fence the old execution. Then make an explicit operator decision:

    Terminal
    php osoni queue:resolve JOB_ID retry --force
php osoni queue:resolve JOB_ID complete --force

    The force flag is an operator assertion, not proof that a remote process died. Never release overlap/uniqueness protection merely because a clock expired. The existing email queue keeps its separate uncertain SMTP-delivery safeguards; scheduling mail:work does not automatically resend uncertain email.

    Timezones, DST, and Missed Schedules

    Persistence uses UTC timestamps. Calendar tasks interpret their configured IANA timezone, independently of the server's display timezone.

    At spring-forward, a nonexistent local time is skipped. At fall-back, a repeated local time runs only at its first occurrence. Elapsed-time intervals remain anchored in UTC.

    skipMissed() is the default: only work within the configured polling tolerance is materialized. runMissed(limit: 1) catches up the latest missed occurrence. Larger catch-up is bounded by the configured ceiling; a restart does not silently replay years of historical work. A newly registered task starts from the current schedule boundary, not an invented historical backlog.

    Worker Management and Timeouts

    Terminal
    php osoni scheduler:list
php osoni scheduler:status
php osoni scheduler:run
php osoni queue:status
php osoni workers:list
php osoni workers:stop WORKER_ID

    Workers register random identities plus host/PID information and update heartbeats. Stale workers are suspected offline, not conclusively dead. Database-backed stop requests work without Unix signals. The worker listing shows the newest 100 registrations by default.

    Terminal
    php osoni queue:work --queue=billing,default --sleep=1 --tries=3
php osoni queue:work --max-jobs=100 --max-time=3600
php osoni queue:work --once

    Lifetime/job-count limits are checked between executions; they do not interrupt arbitrary running PHP. --once exits after at most one eligible execution, including when the selected queue is empty.

    Priorities are integers: 0 low, 1 normal, 2 high, 3 critical. Waiting-time aging prevents fresh high-priority jobs from permanently starving older low-priority jobs. Workers only claim their selected queues.

    Workers use monitored child PHP processes, so the parent can maintain heartbeats. The native proc_open() function must be enabled. Timeouts request cooperative cancellation and quarantine uncertain work; they do not forcibly terminate arbitrary PHP or undo side effects. An uncooperative child can keep its parent occupied until it exits. Use additional workers for other work and a supervisor for hard process deadlines. Handlers should check their execution context between operations and configure network/database timeouts of their own.

    Production Deployment: Linux, Windows, and Docker

    Osoni owns scheduling logic while its processes are alive. It cannot keep itself alive after a machine reboot, crash, or container termination.

    • Linux: supervise separate scheduler and queue processes with systemd or Supervisor. Use the application directory as working directory and an unprivileged service identity. Adapt the supplied systemd template, then enable osoni@scheduler and osoni@queue. Replace its user, paths, and shutdown timeout for your deployment; never start services before configuring and migrating the application database.
    • Windows: use a Windows service wrapper to run the same PHP CLI commands, with an explicit working directory, PHP path, database access, and private storage ACLs.
    • Docker: use separate scheduler and worker services with restart policies, the same deployed code/configuration, and sufficient shutdown grace time.
    • macOS: run the CLI directly for development or supervise it with launchd.

    These are process-lifecycle integrations, not cron replacements containing your application's timetable. No cron or Windows Task Scheduler is required. Use a PHP CLI configuration with appropriate memory limits and extension settings. Recycle long-lived workers during deployments so they load new code.

    For Docker Compose, adapt this example to an existing application image with PHP CLI, the required native extensions, deployed code, and database configuration. It is not a Docker build recipe:

    YAML
    services:
  scheduler:
    image: your-osoni-application:release
    working_dir: /app
    command: ["php", "osoni", "scheduler:work"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 11m
    env_file: .env
  queue:
    image: your-osoni-application:release
    working_dir: /app
    command: ["php", "osoni", "queue:work", "--queue=default,billing"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 11m
    env_file: .env

    Use the same server database for both services and run migrations as a separate deployment step. Supply protected persistent storage for application data/logs. Tune the example's shutdown grace period to exceed your longest job timeout; an orchestrator may still forcibly terminate processes when that period ends.

    Monitoring, Retention, and Troubleshooting

    Queue/scheduler status commands show identifiers and safe runtime metadata, not payloads. Application logs contain structured lifecycle information; exception messages and handler output are not assumed safe to expose.

    For trusted programmatic monitoring, use $app->queue->store()->status() or jobs('pending', 50), which omit payloads and claim credentials. Register listeners on $app->worker->events->on('job.finished', $listener) before starting the worker. Listeners receive safe metadata arrays. Available events are worker.started, worker.stopped, job.claimed, job.started, and job.finished; listener failures are logged without undoing job acknowledgement. Child-process events such as job.started require listeners registered during trusted child bootstrap; in-memory parent listeners are not copied to children.

    Terminal
    php osoni queue:prune --days=30 --limit=100

    Pruning removes bounded terminal history, not active or uncertain work. Keep occurrence deduplication records long enough for recovery; do not manually truncate live tables.

    SymptomCheck
    Worker exits at startupCLI PHP version, enabled proc_open(), database schema and private storage permissions
    Nothing runsSchedule registry, timezone, selected queue, worker heartbeat, availability/backoff
    Job type rejectedExplicit registry loading, validator, versioned job identifier
    Pending occurrence rejected after deploymentDefinition fingerprint and deployed handler compatibility
    Work is uncertainInvestigate acknowledgement loss, old processes, and external effects before resolving
    Database repeatedly failsCheck connectivity/TLS/schema; infrastructure failures stop the worker, so configure supervisor restart delays rather than a tight restart loop
    Billing runs twice after recoveryApplication idempotency/business constraints; queue delivery is not exactly-once

    Tests

    Create your own tests

    Generate a test from the project root:

    Terminal
    php osoni make:test ContactTest

    This creates tests/application/ContactTest.php. If you supply Contact instead, the CLI adds the Test suffix for you. Names must start with an uppercase ASCII letter and contain only letters and digits. Existing files are never overwritten; --force is not supported.

    Open tests/application.php and add the registration line printed by the command. Keep any existing registrations. Do not add a second <?php tag:

    PHP
    require __DIR__ . '/application/ContactTest.php';

    There is no automatic file discovery: an unregistered file will not run. The generator does not edit the registry for you. If an older project does not have tests/application.php, create it with an opening <?php tag and the require line above; its test runner must include the application registry as shown in the current tests/run.php.

    The generated placeholder deliberately fails so an unfinished test cannot appear to pass. Replace its entire contents with a real check, for example:

    PHP
    <?php
declare(strict_types=1);

test('Contact names must contain at least two characters', static function (): void {
    $errors = \Osoni\Validator::errors(['name' => 'A'], [
        'name' => 'required|string|min:2',
    ]);
    check(isset($errors['name']), 'A one-character name should be rejected.');
    same([], \Osoni\Validator::errors(['name' => 'Ada'], [
        'name' => 'required|string|min:2',
    ]));
});

    Run all registered tests, including the framework suite:

    Terminal
    php osoni test

    Look for your test's OK or FAIL line and the final pass/fail summary. Any failed test makes the command exit with code 1. The native helpers are check($condition, $message) for a true condition, same($expected, $actual) for strict equality, and raises($callback, ExceptionClass::class) for an expected exception. Test files are loaded by the runner, not executed directly.

    Write each test as a test('description', static function (): void { ... }); block. Load application classes explicitly with require_once as needed. Do not use the real application's database, mail delivery, or AI service merely to run a test; create isolated fixtures and clean them up in finally. No PHPUnit, Composer packages, test filtering, or separate feature/unit runner is introduced by this generator.

    Terminal
    php osoni test
php osoni routes

    The tests use an isolated temporary SQLite database, test all generators, and briefly start a local HTTP server on an available port. The server is stopped and temporary files are cleaned up. SMTP and IMAP are tested through local protocol fixtures, including native TLS, STARTTLS, authentication, certificate verification, database queue, deduplication, and loss of the SMTP confirmation. No external email is sent. AI tests exercise request mapping, history, streamed SSE framing, errors, truncation, callback cancellation, and native HTTPS through isolated local TLS fixtures. They use no real provider credentials, call no external AI service, and incur no API charges. Authentication tests exercise the real HTTP forms, session and CSRF rotation, email verification, token expiration/reuse, password reset, session revocation, and persistent rate limits on a temporary database. ORM tests check query bindings, identifier validation, CRUD, write guards, fillable/hidden, casts and corrupted stored values, pagination, relationships, manual keys, transactions, and the model generator. Encryption tests check native OpenSSL interoperability, random nonces, byte-level tampering, incorrect keys/contexts, invalid payloads, CLI key generation, and encrypted ORM casts. Bot protection tests check session/form binding, expiration, reuse, honeypot types, bounded session storage, SVG responses, refreshing, and the absence of side effects on all five protected forms. API tests check token hashes, verification, expiration/revocation, password reset, stateless HTTP, JSON errors/body limits, rate limiting, OpenAPI/route registration, CLI scaffolding, and the local Swagger assets and restricted CSP. MySQL has an opt-in disposable-database integration script and a CI service job described in the production chapter. Native local tests do not connect to a live MySQL server; require successful integration results for your deployment. SQL Server has recording-PDO dialect tests and a separate, explicitly enabled live integration script described in its chapter. PostgreSQL likewise has recording-PDO tests, an opt-in live test script, and a dedicated CI service job described above.

    Function reference

    Every public method declared by the framework is listed below, including constructors, magic methods, and low-level integration surfaces. The two protected ORM relationship helpers are included because application models call them. Private implementation helpers and inherited native PHP exception methods are not application APIs.

    Signatures, parameter defaults, public properties, source locations, and PHPDoc array shapes are read from the actual source when this manual is built. Each function has an authored explanation and example; the builder fails if a declared method is missing. Constructors return an object through new, even though PHP constructor signatures have no return type.

    In snippets, $app is the bootstrapped Application; $request is the handler Request; $date is a DateTimeImmutable; $query is a Query; $notes/$note are the model prototype/loaded record from the Model starting point; $file, $pdf, $book, $word, and mail variables are introduced by their feature chapter. Snippets using $__engine illustrate compiler internals, not standalone scripts. Examples with a public method declaration belong inside your subclass.

    Unless an explanation says otherwise, invalid arguments throw InvalidArgumentException/TypeError and I/O/database failures throw exceptions. A void function completes without returning application data; chainable builder returns reuse that builder, while Query filters clone it. Do not catch exceptions just to return a success-shaped fallback.

    Osoni\Ai

    Server-side text conversations and synchronous incremental text streaming for OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Claude Messages, available through $app->ai. Uses native cURL with verified HTTPS and fixed provider URLs; no Composer, public endpoint, conversation storage, logging, retries, or provider fallback. Requests are capped at 4 MiB, responses at 16 MiB including SSE overhead, and individual stream events at 4 MiB. Images, tools, structured output, audio, and reasoning replay are outside this text-only API. Returned text is untrusted; escape it for the output context.

    Starting point

    $ai = $app->ai;

    Ai::__construct()

    public __construct(array $config = [], ?Closure $transport = NULL)

Configuration: provider (openai or anthropic), timeout (1..300 seconds, default 60), max_tokens (1..128000, default 1024), optional ca_file, and openai/anthropic arrays with key and model. Key/model are checked only for the selected provider at call time; no model is silently selected. Optional trusted transport Closure receives URL, list of headers, JSON body, timeout, and a chunk-consumer Closure; it must synchronously deliver successful raw body bytes and throw on transport/non-200 errors.     public chat(array $messages, ?string $provider = NULL, ?string $system = NULL, ?string $model = NULL, ?int $maxTokens = NULL): array

    Send a nonempty list of role/content messages and return exactly provider, id, model, text, finish_reason, input_tokens, and output_tokens. Roles are user or assistant; content must be nonempty UTF-8 text. Supply system instructions separately. Optional provider, system, model, and maxTokens override this call only. Invalid input throws InvalidArgumentException; network, HTTP, protocol, and provider failures throw RuntimeException without raw provider errors. HTTP failures carry their status as the exception code.

    Ai::stream()

    PHP
    public stream(array $messages, callable $onText, ?string $provider = NULL, ?string $system = NULL, ?string $model = NULL, ?int $maxTokens = NULL): array

    Make a streaming request and synchronously call onText(string $delta): void for each nonempty text delta as bytes arrive. UTF-8 SSE framing, LF/CRLF/CR, comments, multiple data lines, and future unrelated events are handled. The returned array has the same seven keys as chat() and includes the assembled text and final usage. Missing terminal events, failed/incomplete network transfers, unsupported output, invalid JSON, and mismatched OpenAI final text throw, even after callbacks have emitted partial text. Callback exceptions cancel the connection and propagate unchanged. No automatic retry occurs, avoiding duplicate output and unexpected charges. This does not create an HTTP SSE response, flush output buffers, or release web session locks.

    Osoni\Auth

    Authentication requires migrated users/auth token/rate-limit/MFA tables and a started native session. MFA enrollment additionally requires a valid APP_KEY through Database encryption. Bootstrap loads config/auth.php: mfa_enrollment_enabled and mfa_enforcement_enabled default to true and require actual PHP booleans. AUTH_MFA_ENROLLMENT_ENABLED=false blocks starting/confirming setup, not existing enrollment or management. AUTH_MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED=false is an emergency-only bypass for new password and OIDC login challenges, retaining secrets/counters/recovery hashes. Management still requires both factors. Changes do not revoke sessions/tokens or promote pending challenges; bypass-created sessions survive restoring enforcement until expiry/revocation. Restart all application processes on all instances after any policy change. The existing controllers add CAPTCHA/CSRF and safe UI flows; direct service calls do not automatically add those layers. AuthException holds safe field errors.

    public static svg(string $text): string

    Return an inline black-on-white SVG with a four-module quiet zone for 1-2953 printable ASCII bytes. Empty, oversized, control-character, and non-ASCII input throws InvalidArgumentException. Render only this generated markup with Osoni raw output, keep the white border intact, and retain a manual-key fallback.     public static capture(): Osoni\Request

    Build a request from PHP server globals, rejecting malformed URLs.     public send(bool $head = false): void

    Set status and headers, then echo buffered content or stream a local file without loading it entirely into memory. HEAD, 1xx, 204 and 304 omit content.     public isReadOnly(string $method): bool

    Return true for GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS, the methods that carry no token.     GET/HEAD/OPTIONS carry no token, and a cross-site page cannot send them
with a token either. Osoni never changes data in a read handler, so a form
can submit these to a state-changing route instead of its POST, which
skips the check. Do not treat them as safe in verifyCsrf.

    Osoni\Storage\SftpDriver

    Native ext-ssh2 driver with pinned SHA-1 host-key identity, password or RSA PEM key-file authentication, existing absolute remote root, directory listings for reliable missing-vs-failure distinction, and lstat symlink refusal. RSA PEM avoids unverified OpenSSH/ECDSA key compatibility. SHA-1 pin format is imposed by ext-ssh2; independently verify it, and use server-side confinement. No guaranteed per-operation deadline is available through this extension.

    Osoni\Worker\Worker

    Supervised shell-free PHP children, private stdin claim tokens, configurable heartbeats, safe lifecycle logging, and unknown-outcome quarantine. Caught handler errors retry only when explicitly retry-safe or RetryableJobFailure; ambiguous crashes remain uncertain. Arbitrary code is never force-killed and declared safely retryable.
